=== cap-interp-01 | The lexer: tokens, positions and every error at once
--- teach
In Programming Languages & Compilers you built Comet one piece at a time: a lexer, a parser, an interpreter, each lesson handing you the earlier pieces already working. This capstone builds the whole language again, as one project that you own from the first line to the last. It is about 2,000 lines of Python by the end, in twelve milestones, and each one leaves you with something that runs and is tested. By the last milestone Comet has lists, maps, loops with `break`, closures, a standard library with `map`, `filter` and `sort`, runtime errors with a call-stack trace, a REPL, and a test runner written in Comet itself.

This first milestone is the **lexer**, the part that turns source text into tokens. You wrote one before. This one has to be good enough to build a real language on: it reports every mistake in the text, not just the first, and every report says exactly where.

### How the milestones work

Every milestone's starter is **the whole project so far**: the previous milestone's solution, unchanged, plus stubs for the new parts. A stub raises `NotImplementedError`, so a part you have not written fails loudly instead of quietly returning something wrong. The checks test the new milestone, and they also re-run the important tests of the earlier ones, so a change that breaks old behaviour fails straight away. That kind of old test is called a **regression test**: a test that catches a feature which used to work and has stopped working.

Keep your own solution from one milestone to the next if you like it better than the given one. What matters is that the names and behaviour in each task stay exactly as specified, because the checks call them.

### Comet, capstone edition

The language is the Comet of the Compilers course, with a few additions that later milestones need. The lexer must know all of them now:

| kind | examples | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `NUMBER` | `0`, `42`, `007` | decimal digits only |
| `STRING` | `"hi\n"` | the token's text is the **decoded** value: no quotes, escapes applied |
| `IDENT` | `total`, `_tmp`, `x2` | a letter or `_`, then letters, digits or `_` |
| `KEYWORD` | `let fn return if else while for in break continue print true false nil and or not` | new: `for`, `in`, `break`, `continue`, `nil` |
| `OP` | `+ - * / % == != < <= > >= = ( ) { } [ ] , ; : ->` | new: `[` and `]` |
| `EOF` | | always last, with empty text |

A `#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. The escapes in strings are `\"`, `\\` and `\n`. A string cannot run past the end of its line. Letters are the plain ASCII letters `a` to `z` and `A` to `Z`, and digits are `0` to `9`.

A token is the dataclass `Token(kind, text, line, col)`, and the line and column count from 1.

### The job, stated precisely

The lexer reads the text from left to right. At each position it skips spaces and comments, or it takes the **longest** piece of text that forms a token, and moves past it. Taking the longest piece is called **[[maximal munch|munch]]**. It is why `<=` is one token and not `<` followed by `=`, and why `letter` is one name and not the keyword `let` followed by `ter`.

In everyday words: you read a sentence and split it into words, and you never split in the middle of a word just because its first half is also a word.

Here is the text `if x>=10{` and what the lexer must produce:

| text | kind | line | col |
|---|---|---|---|
| `if` | KEYWORD | 1 | 1 |
| `x` | IDENT | 1 | 4 |
| `>=` | OP | 1 | 5 |
| `10` | NUMBER | 1 | 7 |
| `{` | OP | 1 | 9 |
| | EOF | 1 | 10 |

The `EOF` token sits one column past the last character. When a parser later says "expected `}`, found end of input", that is the position it points at.

### Design choice: a hand-written scanner

You could write the lexer as one big regular expression, which is what the course's practice problems did once. It is short, and fine for a quick tool. This project writes the scanner by hand, character by character, for three reasons:

1. **Positions.** Every character goes through one method, `advance`, which is the only place that moves the line and column. Nothing can get out of step.
2. **Errors.** At each point the code knows what it was in the middle of (a string, a number), so the message can say what went wrong: "unterminated string" is more useful than "no pattern matched".
3. **Recovery.** A hand-written loop can decide, for each kind of mistake, how much text to skip and where to carry on.

Most production compilers write their lexers by hand for the same reasons: GCC, Clang, Go, Swift and V8 all do. Tools such as `lex` and `flex` generate lexers from regular expressions, and they are used where error messages matter less.

### The data the lexer keeps

The lexer is a small class with a little state:

- `source`, the text, and `pos`, the index of the next character to read;
- `line` and `col`, the position of that next character;
- `tokens`, the list built so far, and `errors`, the mistakes found so far.

Two helpers do all the reading. `peek` looks at a character without consuming it, and `advance` consumes one. This is the **invariant** of the whole class: *`line` and `col` always describe the character at `pos`*. `advance` keeps it true. Reading `x\ny` goes like this:

| before advance | char read | after: pos, line, col |
|---|---|---|
| pos 0, line 1, col 1 | `x` | 1, 1, 2 |
| pos 1, line 1, col 2 | newline | 2, 2, 1 |
| pos 2, line 2, col 1 | `y` | 3, 2, 2 |

A newline moves to the next line and back to column 1. Anything else moves one column right. So a token's position is simply the lexer's line and column **before** it starts reading the token: save them first, then read.

`peek` must be safe at the end of the text. The simplest safe answer past the end is the empty string `""`, which is not any real character.

An alternative is to record only each token's offset (its index in the text), and turn an offset into a line and column when an error is actually printed, by binary search over the positions where lines start. That is cheaper when most tokens never appear in a message, and big compilers do it. Here, counting as you go is simpler, and just as fast in big-O terms.

### Design choice: keep going after a mistake

The Compilers course's lexer stopped at the first bad character. That is annoying in practice: fix one mistake, run again, meet the next one. This lexer records each mistake as a `LexError` in `errors` and **carries on**. That is called **error recovery**. The hard part is choosing where to carry on, so that one mistake does not cause a flood of false ones:

| mistake | where it is reported | where scanning carries on |
|---|---|---|
| a character that starts no token, such as `@` | at that character | just after it |
| a string with no closing quote before the end of the line | at the opening quote | at the end of that line |
| an unknown escape, such as `\q` | at the backslash | just after the escape, still inside the string |

Each choice skips as little as possible. A string that is not closed on its line is given up at the line's end, because strings in Comet never cross lines: the next line is almost certainly ordinary code again.

`scan()` returns both lists as a pair, `(tokens, errors)`. The old interface is kept as a small function: `tokenize(source)` scans, and if there were errors it raises the first one, otherwise it returns the tokens. Later milestones use whichever fits.

### Messages people can act on

A good message says **where** (line and column), **what** was found, and, when it can, **what to do**. People arrive at Comet from other languages and type their habits, so the lexer recognises four characters and adds a hint:

```text
1:9: unexpected character "'" (strings use double quotes)
2:7: unexpected character '&' (use 'and')
```

The `repr` of a one-character Python string gives the quoted character: `'@'` for most characters, and `"'"` for a single quote. So the message format is "unexpected character" followed by the `repr`.

The last piece of the milestone shows a mistake in context: the source line, and a **caret**, the `^` mark, under the column. For line 2, column 5 of this text:

```text
let a = 1;
let @ = 2;
```

the result is two lines, `let @ = 2;` and then four spaces and `^`. There is one trap: a tab. A terminal shows a tab as several columns, so if the source line had a tab before column 5, four spaces would put the caret in the wrong place. The fix is to copy each tab from the source line into the padding and use a space for every other character. Then the terminal moves the caret exactly as far as it moved the text. See the [[tab note|tabs]].

### Why the scanner is correct, and why it stops

- **It stops.** Every pass of the main loop consumes at least one character: whitespace is advanced over, a comment consumes its `#`, every token consumes its first character, and a bad character is skipped. So after at most n passes, for n characters, `pos` reaches the end.
- **Positions are right.** By the invariant, the position saved at the start of a token is the position of its first character.
- **Tokens are in order.** They are appended as the text is read, from left to right.

### What it costs

Each character is advanced over once and peeked at a constant number of times, so scanning n characters takes Θ(n) time, and the tokens take Θ(n) space. One slip turns this quadratic: building a slice of the rest of the text, such as `source[pos:]`, on every peek. Each slice copies up to n characters, so n peeks copy about n²/2. On a 200,000-character file that is 20 billion copies. The checks lex a file that size.

### How to test a lexer

Test with small texts whose answer you can write by hand, one idea per test: each kind of token, maximal munch (`<=`, `letter`), positions after a newline, the `EOF` position, and each kind of error with its exact message and position. Then test two errors in one text, to prove that scanning carried on. Finally, one large input to prove the cost is linear.

### Where it is used

- Every compiler, interpreter, syntax highlighter and code formatter starts with a lexer.
- [[Editors highlight code as you type|incremental]], so their lexers must be fast and must survive broken text: you are always halfway through typing something.
- Telemetry command languages on spacecraft ground systems start the same way: a command line typed by an operator is split into tokens, and a mistyped command must be reported with its position before anything is sent.

**Watch out:** four classic lexer bugs.

- Testing `ch in "0123456789"` when `ch` can be `""`. In Python the empty string is inside every string, so at the end of the text the test is still true, and a loop that reads digits tries to read past the end and crashes with an `IndexError`. Test against a **set** of characters instead, where `""` is not a member. The same goes for letters.
- Forgetting to reset the column to 1 after a newline, so every position after line 1 is off.
- Forgetting the `EOF` token, or giving it a position that is not just past the end.
- Using Python's `str.isdigit` or `str.isalpha`. They accept far more than ASCII: `"²".isdigit()` is true, and `int("²")` then fails. See the [[Unicode note|unicode]].

::: context munch Maximal munch
Maximal munch means: at each point, take the longest piece of text that is a valid token. It is the rule nearly every lexer uses, and it makes lexing deterministic, with no guessing and no going back. It has one famous cost. In C++ before 2011, `vector<vector<int>>` did not compile, because `>>` was munched as the shift operator. Programmers had to write `> >` with a space, until the C++11 standard added a special rule for exactly this case.
:::

::: context tabs Why the caret copies tabs
A tab character does not have a fixed width. A terminal moves the cursor to the next tab stop, usually a multiple of 8 columns, so one tab can look like 1 to 8 spaces depending on where it starts. The lexer counts it as one column, which is what the column in a message means. To draw the caret, copying the tab keeps the padding exactly as wide as the text above it, whatever the terminal's tab stops are. Python's own traceback uses a similar trick when it underlines the part of a line that failed.
:::

::: context incremental Lexers inside editors
An editor that colours code cannot re-lex a 10,000-line file on every keystroke. Editors keep the lexer's state at the start of each line, and after an edit they re-lex from the changed line until the state matches what it was before, which is usually a line or two later. That only works when the lexer never gives up on broken text, which is why recovery matters so much there. Tree-sitter, used by GitHub and many editors, is built around the same idea.
:::

::: context unicode Unicode digits and letters
Unicode has hundreds of characters that Python calls digits or letters: superscript two, Arabic-Indic digits, Greek and Cyrillic letters. `str.isdigit()` returns true for all of those digits, but `int()` only accepts some of them. Comet keeps its identifiers and numbers to plain ASCII, which avoids look-alike names (a Latin `a` and a Cyrillic `а` look identical but are different names), a real security problem called a homoglyph attack.
:::
--- task
The starter gives the token table as constants (`KEYWORDS`, `TWO_CHAR`, `ONE_CHAR`, `ESCAPES`, `DIGITS`, `LETTERS`, `LEX_HINTS`), the `Token` dataclass, and the errors `StaticError(message, line, col)` and its subclass `LexError`. A `StaticError` keeps `message`, `line` and `col`, and `str()` of it is `"line:col: message"`. Write:

- `class Lexer`, made with `Lexer(source)`, with a method `scan()` that returns the pair `(tokens, errors)`:
  - `tokens` is every token of the text as a `Token(kind, text, line, col)`, in order, ending with one `EOF` token (text `""`) positioned just after the last character. Kinds and texts follow the lesson's table. A `STRING` token's text is the decoded value, and its position is the opening quote. Spaces, tabs, `\r`, newlines and `#` comments make no tokens. Use maximal munch for names and for the two-character operators.
  - `errors` is every mistake, as a `LexError`, in the order found. Scanning always carries on:
    - a character that starts no token: message `unexpected character ` followed by the character's Python `repr` (for example `unexpected character '@'`), at that character; if the character is a key of `LEX_HINTS`, add a space and the hint in brackets: `unexpected character '&' (use 'and')`. Skip the character.
    - a string with no closing quote before a newline or the end: `unterminated string`, at the opening quote. It makes no token, and scanning carries on at the newline.
    - a backslash followed by a character that is not `"`, `\` or `n`: `unknown escape \q` (with that character), at the backslash. Skip both characters and carry on inside the string.
- `tokenize(source)`: return the tokens, or raise the first `LexError` if there were any.
- `point_at(source, line, col)`: return two lines joined by a newline: line number `line` of the source (the empty string if there is no such line), and a caret `^` preceded by `col - 1` characters of padding. The padding copies each tab among the first `col - 1` characters of the line and uses a space for everything else, including columns past the end of the line.

Lexing must take linear time: a check lexes about 200,000 characters.
--- starter
"""Comet: a small programming language, built in layers.

    source text -> Lexer -> tokens -> Parser -> syntax tree
                -> Resolver -> Interpreter -> printed output

Each layer only talks to the one after it, so each can be tested alone.
"""
import operator
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

    "let", "fn", "return", "if", "else", "while", "for", "in", "break",
    "continue", "print", "true", "false", "nil", "and", "or", "not",
}
TWO_CHAR = {"==", "!=", "<=", ">=", "->"}
ONE_CHAR = set("+-*/%<>=(){}[],;:")
ESCAPES = {'"': '"', "\\": "\\", "n": "\n"}

LETTERS = set("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ_")

    "'": "strings use double quotes",
    "&": "use 'and'",
    "|": "use 'or'",
    "!": "use 'not', or '!=' for not equal",
}


@dataclass

    text: str   # the source text; for a STRING, the decoded value
    line: int   # counted from 1
    col: int    # counted from 1

        self.line = line
        self.col = col

        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Lexer")

        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 1: Lexer.scan")

--- solution
"""Comet: a small programming language, built in layers.

    source text -> Lexer -> tokens -> Parser -> syntax tree
                -> Resolver -> Interpreter -> printed output

Each layer only talks to the one after it, so each can be tested alone.
"""
import operator
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


# ============================================================================
# Tokens and the lexer
# ============================================================================

KEYWORDS = {
    "let", "fn", "return", "if", "else", "while", "for", "in", "break",
    "continue", "print", "true", "false", "nil", "and", "or", "not",
}
TWO_CHAR = {"==", "!=", "<=", ">=", "->"}
ONE_CHAR = set("+-*/%<>=(){}[],;:")
ESCAPES = {'"': '"', "\\": "\\", "n": "\n"}
DIGITS = set("0123456789")
LETTERS = set("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ_")
# Characters people type from other languages, and what Comet wants instead.
LEX_HINTS = {
    "'": "strings use double quotes",
    "&": "use 'and'",
    "|": "use 'or'",
    "!": "use 'not', or '!=' for not equal",
}


@dataclass
class Token:
    kind: str   # NUMBER, STRING, IDENT, KEYWORD, OP or EOF
    text: str   # the source text; for a STRING, the decoded value
    line: int   # counted from 1
    col: int    # counted from 1


class StaticError(Exception):
    """A mistake found before the program runs. Prints as "line:col: message"."""

    def __init__(self, message, line, col):
        super().__init__(f"{line}:{col}: {message}")
        self.message = message
        self.line = line
        self.col = col


class LexError(StaticError):
    """A character sequence that is not a Comet token."""


class Lexer:
    """Turns source text into tokens. It keeps going after a mistake, so one
    scan reports every lexing error, each with its line and column."""

    def __init__(self, source):
        self.source = source
        self.pos = 0          # index of the next character to read
        self.line = 1         # where that character is, for messages
        self.col = 1
        self.tokens = []
        self.errors = []

    def peek(self, ahead=0):
        """A character ahead of the read position, or "" past the end."""
        i = self.pos + ahead
        return self.source[i] if i < len(self.source) else ""

    def advance(self):
        """Consumes one character and keeps line and col in step with it."""
        ch = self.source[self.pos]
        self.pos += 1
        if ch == "\n":
            self.line += 1
            self.col = 1
        else:
            self.col += 1
        return ch

    def scan(self):
        """Returns (tokens, errors): every token ending with EOF, and every LexError."""
        while self.pos < len(self.source):
            self.scan_token()
        self.tokens.append(Token("EOF", "", self.line, self.col))
        return self.tokens, self.errors

    def scan_token(self):
        line, col = self.line, self.col
        ch = self.peek()
        if ch in " \t\r\n":
            self.advance()
        elif ch == "#":
            while self.peek() not in ("", "\n"):
                self.advance()
        elif ch in DIGITS:
            self.number(line, col)
        elif ch in LETTERS:
            self.word(line, col)
        elif ch == '"':
            self.string(line, col)
        elif ch + self.peek(1) in TWO_CHAR:
            text = self.advance() + self.advance()
            self.tokens.append(Token("OP", text, line, col))
        elif ch in ONE_CHAR:
            self.tokens.append(Token("OP", self.advance(), line, col))
        else:
            self.advance()   # skip it, report it, and carry on
            message = f"unexpected character {ch!r}"
            if ch in LEX_HINTS:
                message += f" ({LEX_HINTS[ch]})"
            self.errors.append(LexError(message, line, col))

    def number(self, line, col):
        start = self.pos
        while self.peek() in DIGITS:
            self.advance()
        self.tokens.append(Token("NUMBER", self.source[start:self.pos], line, col))

    def word(self, line, col):
        start = self.pos
        while self.peek() in LETTERS or self.peek() in DIGITS:
            self.advance()
        text = self.source[start:self.pos]
        kind = "KEYWORD" if text in KEYWORDS else "IDENT"
        self.tokens.append(Token(kind, text, line, col))

    def string(self, line, col):
        """A string literal. The token's text is the decoded value."""
        self.advance()  # the opening quote
        chars = []
        while True:
            ch = self.peek()
            if ch in ("", "\n"):
                # Strings never span lines, so the rest of this line is lost.
                self.errors.append(LexError("unterminated string", line, col))
                return
            if ch == '"':
                self.advance()
                break
            if ch == "\\":
                at_line, at_col = self.line, self.col
                self.advance()
                code = self.peek()
                if code in ESCAPES:
                    chars.append(ESCAPES[self.advance()])
                elif code not in ("", "\n"):
                    self.advance()
                    self.errors.append(LexError(f"unknown escape \\{code}", at_line, at_col))
                continue
            chars.append(self.advance())
        self.tokens.append(Token("STRING", "".join(chars), line, col))


def tokenize(source):
    """The tokens of source; raises the first LexError if there is one."""
    tokens, errors = Lexer(source).scan()
    if errors:
        raise errors[0]
    return tokens


def point_at(source, line, col):
    """Two lines: source line `line`, and a caret under column `col`.
    Tabs before the column are copied, so the caret lines up in a terminal."""
    lines = source.split("\n")
    text = lines[line - 1] if 1 <= line <= len(lines) else ""
    pad = "".join("\t" if c == "\t" else " " for c in text[:col - 1])
    return text + "\n" + pad.ljust(col - 1) + "^"
--- hint
Keep `pos`, `line` and `col` in the lexer, and write `peek(ahead)` (return `""` past the end) and `advance()` (consume one character; a newline moves to the next line and column 1). Then `scan()` loops while characters are left, calling one `scan_token()` method, and appends `EOF` at the end.
--- hint
In `scan_token`, save `line, col = self.line, self.col` first: that is the token's position. Then decide by the first character: whitespace, `#`, a digit, a letter, a quote, a two-character operator (`ch + self.peek(1) in TWO_CHAR`), a one-character operator, or an error. Numbers and names loop `while self.peek() in DIGITS` (a set, so `""` is never in it).
--- hint
For strings, loop: a newline or `""` means record `unterminated string` at the saved position and return with no token; a quote ends the string; a backslash saves its own position, advances, and either decodes the escape with `ESCAPES` or records `unknown escape` and skips the character. For `point_at`, build the padding from `text[:col - 1]` and then `ljust(col - 1)` for columns past the end.
--- check case | A let statement
[(t.kind, t.text) for t in tokenize("let x = 42;")]
=> [("KEYWORD", "let"), ("IDENT", "x"), ("OP", "="), ("NUMBER", "42"), ("OP", ";"), ("EOF", "")]
--- check case | Positions, including after a newline and the EOF token
[(t.text, t.line, t.col) for t in tokenize("if x>=10{\n  print y;\n}")]
=> [("if", 1, 1), ("x", 1, 4), (">=", 1, 5), ("10", 1, 7), ("{", 1, 9), ("print", 2, 3), ("y", 2, 9), (";", 2, 10), ("}", 3, 1), ("", 3, 2)]
--- check case | Keywords against names, with maximal munch
[(t.kind, t.text) for t in tokenize("for in nil letter _x2 break continue format")][:-1]
=> [("KEYWORD", "for"), ("KEYWORD", "in"), ("KEYWORD", "nil"), ("IDENT", "letter"), ("IDENT", "_x2"), ("KEYWORD", "break"), ("KEYWORD", "continue"), ("IDENT", "format")]
--- check case | Every operator, and two-character ones taken whole
[t.text for t in tokenize("a<=b!=c->[1]==<>=%{},;:*/-+")][:-1]
=> ["a", "<=", "b", "!=", "c", "->", "[", "1", "]", "==", "<", ">=", "%", "{", "}", ",", ";", ":", "*", "/", "-", "+"]
--- check case | Strings are decoded and positioned at their quote
[(t.kind, t.text, t.col) for t in tokenize('x = "a\\"b\\\\c\\nd" + "";')][2:5]
=> [("STRING", 'a"b\\c\nd', 5), ("OP", "+", 18), ("STRING", "", 20)]
--- check case | Comments are skipped, but a # inside a string is kept
[t.text for t in tokenize('print "#1"; # a comment\n# another\nprint 2;')]
=> ["print", "#1", ";", "print", "2", ";", ""]
--- check case | A number or name at the very end of the text
[(t.kind, t.text) for t in tokenize("x1 99")]
=> [("IDENT", "x1"), ("NUMBER", "99"), ("EOF", "")]
?? At the end of the text peek() returns "". If the digit test is `in "0123456789"`, the empty string passes it and the loop reads past the end; test against a set.
--- check case | Empty text is just EOF at 1:1
[(t.kind, t.line, t.col) for t in tokenize("")]
=> [("EOF", 1, 1)]
--- check case | Every bad character is reported, and scanning carries on
(lambda r: ([str(e) for e in r[1]], [t.text for t in r[0]]))(Lexer("let @x = 1 $ 2;\n  ~").scan())
=> (["1:5: unexpected character '@'", "1:12: unexpected character '$'", "2:3: unexpected character '~'"], ["let", "x", "=", "1", "2", ";", ""])
--- check case | Hints for characters from other languages
[str(e) for e in Lexer("a && b || !c\nx = 'hi';").scan()[1]]

+++ practice | An assembly-line lexer
--- task
A tiny assembly language writes one instruction per line, like `ADDI r1, r2, -5 ; add minus five`. Write `lex_asm(line)` that returns a list of `(kind, text)` pairs:

- The first word is the instruction name, kind `"NAME"`: capital letters `A` to `Z` only.
- A register is `r` followed by one or more digits, kind `"REG"`, for example `r12`.
- A whole number, kind `"INT"`, is one or more digits, with an optional `-` straight in front: `-5`, `40`.
- A comma is `("COMMA", ",")`.
- Spaces separate items and make nothing. A `;` starts a comment to the end of the line.
- Anything else raises `ValueError` with the message `col N: unexpected 'c'`, where N is the column (from 1) of the bad character and `c` the character.

For example, `lex_asm("ADDI r1, r2, -5 ; add")` gives `[("NAME", "ADDI"), ("REG", "r1"), ("COMMA", ","), ("REG", "r2"), ("COMMA", ","), ("INT", "-5")]`. An empty line, or a line that is only a comment, gives `[]`.
--- starter
def lex_asm(line):
    return []
--- solution
UPPER = set("ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ")
DIGITS = set("0123456789")


def lex_asm(line):
    out = []
    i = 0
    n = len(line)
    while i < n:
        ch = line[i]
        if ch == " ":
            i += 1
        elif ch == ";":
            break
        elif ch == ",":
            out.append(("COMMA", ","))
            i += 1
        elif ch in UPPER:
            j = i
            while j < n and line[j] in UPPER:
                j += 1
            out.append(("NAME", line[i:j]))
            i = j
        elif ch == "r" and i + 1 < n and line[i + 1] in DIGITS:
            j = i + 1
            while j < n and line[j] in DIGITS:
                j += 1
            out.append(("REG", line[i:j]))
            i = j
        elif ch in DIGITS or (ch == "-" and i + 1 < n and line[i + 1] in DIGITS):
            j = i + 1
            while j < n and line[j] in DIGITS:
                j += 1
            out.append(("INT", line[i:j]))
            i = j
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"col {i + 1}: unexpected '{ch}'")
    return out
--- hint
Walk the line with an index `i`. Decide by the character at `i`: a space, `;`, a comma, a capital letter, `r` followed by a digit, or a digit (or `-` followed by a digit). Anything else is the error.
--- hint
For a run of capitals or digits, move a second index `j` forward while the character is in the set, take `line[i:j]`, and set `i = j`. The column in the error is `i + 1`.
--- check case | The example
lex_asm("ADDI r1, r2, -5 ; add")
=> [("NAME", "ADDI"), ("REG", "r1"), ("COMMA", ","), ("REG", "r2"), ("COMMA", ","), ("INT", "-5")]
--- check case | Numbers, big registers and no spaces
lex_asm("LOAD r15,40,-300")
=> [("NAME", "LOAD"), ("REG", "r15"), ("COMMA", ","), ("INT", "40"), ("COMMA", ","), ("INT", "-300")]
--- check case | Empty and comment-only lines
(lex_asm(""), lex_asm("   ; nothing here"), lex_asm("HALT"))
=> ([], [], [("NAME", "HALT")])
--- check test | A bad character names its column
__import__("unittest").TestCase().assertRaisesRegex(ValueError, "^col 9: unexpected '#'$", lex_asm, "MOV r1, #5") is None
--- check test | A lone minus or a lower-case name is an error
raises(ValueError, lambda: lex_asm("SUB r1, - 5")) and raises(ValueError, lambda: lex_asm("add r1"))

+++ practice | From an offset to a line and a column
--- task
Error messages need a line and a column, but some tools only record a character's offset: its index in the text, from 0. Write `line_col(source, offset)` that returns the pair `(line, col)`, both counted from 1, of the character at that offset. A newline character belongs to the line it ends. The offset `len(source)` is allowed too: it is the position just after the last character, where an "end of input" error points. Any other offset outside the text raises `ValueError`.

For example, in `"ab\ncd"` the offset 0 is `(1, 1)`, the offset 2 (the newline) is `(1, 3)`, the offset 3 is `(2, 1)`, and the offset 5 is `(2, 3)`.
--- starter
def line_col(source, offset):
    return (1, offset)
--- solution
def line_col(source, offset):
    if not 0 <= offset <= len(source):
        raise ValueError(f"offset {offset} is outside the text")
    line = source.count("\n", 0, offset) + 1
    start = source.rfind("\n", 0, offset) + 1
    return (line, offset - start + 1)
--- hint
The line is 1 plus the number of newlines before the offset. The column is how far the offset is from the start of its line, plus 1.
--- hint
`source.count("\n", 0, offset)` counts newlines before the offset, and `source.rfind("\n", 0, offset)` finds the last one before it (or -1, which conveniently makes the line start 0).
--- check case | The examples
[line_col("ab\ncd", k) for k in (0, 2, 3, 5)]
=> [(1, 1), (1, 3), (2, 1), (2, 3)]
--- check case | Empty lines and a text that ends in a newline
[line_col("\n\nx\n", k) for k in (0, 1, 2, 3, 4)]
=> [(1, 1), (2, 1), (3, 1), (3, 2), (4, 1)]
--- check case | The empty text
line_col("", 0)
=> (1, 1)
--- check test | Offsets outside the text
raises(ValueError, lambda: line_col("abc", 4)) and raises(ValueError, lambda: line_col("abc", -1))

+++ practice | Longest match for operators
--- task
Some languages have many operators that start alike: `<`, `<=`, `<<` and `<<=`. Write `split_ops(text, ops)` that splits a string of operator characters into operators using maximal munch: at each point take the longest operator in the set `ops` that the text starts with there. Spaces separate operators and make nothing. If no operator in `ops` starts at some point, raise `ValueError` with the message `no operator at col N` (N from 1).

For example, with `ops = {"<", "<=", "<<", "<<=", "="}`, `split_ops("<<=<", ops)` is `["<<=", "<"]` and `split_ops("< <=", ops)` is `["<", "<="]`.
--- starter
def split_ops(text, ops):
    return list(text)
--- solution
def split_ops(text, ops):
    longest = max((len(op) for op in ops), default=0)
    out = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(text):
        if text[i] == " ":
            i += 1
            continue
        for size in range(min(longest, len(text) - i), 0, -1):
            if text[i:i + size] in ops:
                out.append(text[i:i + size])
                i += size
                break
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"no operator at col {i + 1}")
    return out
--- hint
At each position, try the longest possible length first and shrink: the first slice that is in `ops` is the longest match.
--- hint
A `for ... else` is handy: the `else` runs only when the loop finished without `break`, which is exactly "no operator matched".
--- check case | The examples
(split_ops("<<=<", {"<", "<=", "<<", "<<=", "="}), split_ops("< <=", {"<", "<=", "<<", "<<=", "="}))
=> (["<<=", "<"], ["<", "<="])
--- check case | Greedy even when a shorter split would also work
split_ops("<<<=", {"<", "<=", "<<", "<<="})
=> ["<<", "<="]
--- check case | Three-character operators and spaces
split_ops("===  !== ==", {"=", "==", "===", "!=", "!=="})
=> ["===", "!==", "=="]
--- check test | An unknown character names its column
__import__("unittest").TestCase().assertRaisesRegex(ValueError, "^no operator at col 3$", split_ops, "<=?", {"<", "<="}) is None
--- check case | Empty text
split_ops("", {"<"})
=> []

+++ practice | Numbers with digit separators
--- task
Python and many other languages let you write `1_000_000` to make big numbers readable. Write `read_number(text)` that returns the value of such a number literal as an int, or raises `ValueError` when it is not one. The rules:

- Only digits and underscores are allowed, and there must be at least one digit.
- An underscore must sit between two digits: not first, not last, and never two in a row.
- A number with more than one digit may not start with `0` (so `0` is fine, `007` is not; `0_0` is not either).

For example, `read_number("1_000")` is `1000` and `read_number("0")` is `0`, while `"_1"`, `"1_"`, `"1__0"`, `""`, `"007"` and `"12a"` all raise `ValueError`.
--- starter
def read_number(text):
    return int(text)
--- solution
DIGITS = set("0123456789")


def read_number(text):
    if not text or any(c not in DIGITS and c != "_" for c in text):
        raise ValueError(f"not a number: {text!r}")
    if text[0] == "_" or text[-1] == "_" or "__" in text:
        raise ValueError(f"misplaced underscore: {text!r}")
    digits = text.replace("_", "")
    if len(digits) > 1 and digits[0] == "0":
        raise ValueError(f"leading zero: {text!r}")
    return int(digits)
--- hint
Check the rules one at a time, each with its own test: only allowed characters and not empty; no underscore at either end or doubled; then no leading zero once the underscores are removed.
--- hint
Test characters against a set of digits rather than with `str.isdigit()`, which accepts Unicode digits such as `"²"`.
--- check case | Valid numbers
[read_number(t) for t in ["1_000", "0", "42", "1_2_3", "9999_9999"]]
=> [1000, 0, 42, 123, 99999999]
--- check test | Underscores in the wrong place
all(raises(ValueError, lambda t=t: read_number(t)) for t in ["_1", "1_", "1__0", "_"])
--- check test | Empty, letters and signs
all(raises(ValueError, lambda t=t: read_number(t)) for t in ["", "12a", "-5", " 1", "1.5"])
--- check test | Leading zeros
all(raises(ValueError, lambda t=t: read_number(t)) for t in ["007", "0_0", "01"]) and read_number("10") == 10
--- check test | Unicode digits are not accepted
raises(ValueError, lambda: read_number("1²"))

For `"go now\n to"` it should return `[("go", 1, 1), ("now", 1, 4), ("to", 2, 2)]`.

It gets the first line right, but every column on the later lines is one too small. Find the bug and fix it.

def word_positions(text):

+++ practice | A query lexer that reports everything
--- task
A telemetry dashboard filters readings with queries like `speed > 7.5 and name == "Vega"`. Write `lex_query(text)` that returns `(tokens, errors)`, and keeps going after every mistake:

- `tokens` is a list of `(kind, text, line, col)` tuples, line and col from 1, positions at the token's first character:
  - `"NUMBER"`: digits, optionally followed by `.` and one or more digits (`7`, `7.5`). A `.` not followed by a digit is not part of the number.
  - `"STRING"`: text in double quotes, no escapes; the token's text is what is between the quotes.
  - `"KEYWORD"` for `and`, `or`, `not`; otherwise `"NAME"` for a letter or `_` followed by letters, digits or `_` (ASCII only).
  - `"OP"` for `==`, `!=`, `<=`, `>=`, `<`, `>`, `(`, `)`, with longest match.
- There is no end token. Spaces and newlines make nothing.
- `errors` is a list of strings `"line:col: message"`: `unexpected 'c'` for a character that starts nothing (skip it), and `unterminated string` at the opening quote when a newline or the end comes before the closing quote (scanning carries on at the newline).

For example, `lex_query('a >= 2 @ b')` gives the tokens `[("NAME", "a", 1, 1), ("OP", ">=", 1, 3), ("NUMBER", "2", 1, 6), ("NAME", "b", 1, 10)]` and the errors `["1:8: unexpected '@'"]`.
--- starter
def lex_query(text):
    return [], []
--- solution
DIGITS = set("0123456789")
START = set("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ_")
KEYWORDS = {"and", "or", "not"}
TWO = {"==", "!=", "<=", ">="}
ONE = set("<>()")


def lex_query(text):
    tokens, errors = [], []
    i, line, col = 0, 1, 1
    n = len(text)

    def take(j):
        nonlocal i, line, col
        while i < j:
            if text[i] == "\n":
                line, col = line + 1, 1
            else:
                col += 1
            i += 1

    while i < n:
        ch = text[i]
        at = (line, col)
        if ch in " \n":
            take(i + 1)
        elif ch in DIGITS:
            j = i
            while j < n and text[j] in DIGITS:
                j += 1
            if j + 1 < n and text[j] == "." and text[j + 1] in DIGITS:
                j += 1
                while j < n and text[j] in DIGITS:
                    j += 1
            tokens.append(("NUMBER", text[i:j], *at))
            take(j)
        elif ch in START:
            j = i
            while j < n and (text[j] in START or text[j] in DIGITS):
                j += 1
            word = text[i:j]
            tokens.append(("KEYWORD" if word in KEYWORDS else "NAME", word, *at))
            take(j)
        elif ch == '"':
            j = i + 1
            while j < n and text[j] not in '"\n':
                j += 1
            if j < n and text[j] == '"':
                tokens.append(("STRING", text[i + 1:j], *at))
                take(j + 1)
            else:
                errors.append(f"{at[0]}:{at[1]}: unterminated string")
                take(j)
        elif text[i:i + 2] in TWO:
            tokens.append(("OP", text[i:i + 2], *at))
            take(i + 2)
        elif ch in ONE:
            tokens.append(("OP", ch, *at))
            take(i + 1)
        else:
            errors.append(f"{at[0]}:{at[1]}: unexpected '{ch}'")
            take(i + 1)
    return tokens, errors
--- hint
Use one helper that moves the index forward to a given point and updates line and column as it goes (a newline moves to column 1 of the next line). Save `(line, col)` before each token.
--- hint
For a number, read digits; then only if the next character is `.` **and** the one after it is a digit, take the dot and more digits. For a string, search for the closing quote but stop at a newline; if you stopped without a quote, record the error and move to where you stopped.
--- check case | The example
lex_query('a >= 2 @ b')
=> ([("NAME", "a", 1, 1), ("OP", ">=", 1, 3), ("NUMBER", "2", 1, 6), ("NAME", "b", 1, 10)], ["1:8: unexpected '@'"])
--- check case | A full query with a decimal, a string and keywords
lex_query('speed > 7.5 and not (name == "Vega")')[0]
=> [("NAME", "speed", 1, 1), ("OP", ">", 1, 7), ("NUMBER", "7.5", 1, 9), ("KEYWORD", "and", 1, 13), ("KEYWORD", "not", 1, 17), ("OP", "(", 1, 21), ("NAME", "name", 1, 22), ("OP", "==", 1, 27), ("STRING", "Vega", 1, 30), ("OP", ")", 1, 36)]
--- check case | A dot that is not a decimal point
lex_query("7. x")
=> ([("NUMBER", "7", 1, 1), ("NAME", "x", 1, 4)], ["1:2: unexpected '.'"])
--- check case | Unterminated strings, on two lines, and lexing goes on
lex_query('a == "x\nb != "y')
=> ([("NAME", "a", 1, 1), ("OP", "==", 1, 3), ("NAME", "b", 2, 1), ("OP", "!=", 2, 3)], ["1:6: unterminated string", "2:6: unterminated string"])
--- check case | Several errors in one query
lex_query("x & y | z")[1]
=> ["1:3: unexpected '&'", "1:7: unexpected '|'"]

=== cap-interp-02 | A Pratt parser for expressions
--- teach
Last milestone the lexer turned text into a flat list of tokens. A program is not flat, though: in `1 + 2 * 3` the multiplication happens first, so the `*` sits inside the `+`. This milestone builds the part that finds that structure for expressions, the **parser**, and it uses a technique you have not written before: **Pratt parsing**, where one short loop and one table of operator strengths replace a whole ladder of functions.

### The tree, and why it carries positions

The parser's output is a **syntax tree** (an AST, for abstract syntax tree): one node per operation, with its operands as children. The starter gives the node classes. They are the Compilers course's dataclasses, plus four new expression kinds:

| node | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| `Nil()` | the value nil | `nil` |
| `Index(target, index)` | one item of a list, string or map | `xs[0]` |
| `ListLit(items)` | a list literal | `[1, 2, 3]` |
| `MapLit(pairs)` | a map literal; `pairs` is a list of `(key, value)` tuples of nodes | `{"a": 1}` |

Every node also has a `line` and a `col`, inherited from a base class `Node`. Later milestones point runtime errors at them. They are declared with `field(default=0, kw_only=True, compare=False)`:

- `kw_only=True` puts them after the node's own fields and makes them keyword-only, so `Num(3)` still works and a position is given as `Num(3, line=1, col=5)`. See the [[dataclass note|kwonly]].
- `compare=False` leaves them out of `==`. A test can then compare the tree from `1+2` with `Binary("+", Num(1), Num(2))` and care only about its shape.

The printed form used by the tests is a **prefix expression**, sometimes called an [[S-expression|sexp]]: every node is written as brackets holding its operator and then its children. `1 + 2 * x` is `(+ 1 (* 2 x))`. It shows the grouping at a glance, so a whole tree fits in one line of a test. The starter gives `group(head, *parts)`, which builds `(head part part …)`, and `quote(text)`, which writes a string the way Comet source does, in quotes and with escapes.

### The grammar, as a table of strengths

Comet's expression grammar from the Compilers course was a ladder of rules, one per level: `or`, `and`, `not`, comparison, sum, product, unary, call. The same information fits in a table. Each operator gets a **binding power**: how strongly it holds on to the operands next to it. Stronger operators grab their operands first.

| power | operators | kind |
|---|---|---|
| `OR` = 1 | `or` | binary, left to right |
| `AND` = 2 | `and` | binary, left to right |
| `NOT` = 3 | `not` | prefix |
| `COMPARE` = 4 | `== != < <= > >=` | binary, no chaining |
| `SUM` = 5 | `+ -` | binary, left to right |
| `PRODUCT` = 6 | `* / %` | binary, left to right |
| `UNARY` = 7 | `-` in front | prefix |
| `POSTFIX` = 8 | `f(…)` and `x[…]` | after an operand |

The starter defines these as constants, plus `INFIX`, a dictionary from each operator that can come **after** an operand to its power. `(` and `[` are in `INFIX` too: a call and an index both follow a complete operand, just as `+` does. `LOWEST` = 0 is below everything.

### Why not the ladder

The Compilers course wrote one function per rung of the ladder: `or_expr` called `and_expr`, which called `not_expr`, and so on down to `primary`. That works, and it is still how many parsers are written. It has two costs that grow with the language. Every new level of precedence means a new function, and the order of the calls is the precedence, spread over the whole file. And even the simplest expression, a lone `7`, goes down all eight rungs before anything happens.

Two other classic methods were rejected too. A **parser generator** (yacc, ANTLR) builds a parser from a grammar file, which is a second language to learn and gives poor error messages unless you work hard at them. Dijkstra's [[shunting-yard algorithm|shunting]] uses an explicit stack of operators and is excellent for plain arithmetic, but calls, indexes, literals and good error positions fit awkwardly into it.

Pratt parsing keeps the precedence in one table, handles prefix, infix and postfix operators with the same loop, and a lone `7` costs one function call.

### The Pratt loop

In everyday words: read one operand. Then look at the next operator. If it binds more strongly than whatever is waiting on our left, it takes our operand as its left side, and the result becomes our new operand. Repeat until an operator is too weak, and hand the operand back.

As code, the heart of it is a function `expression(power)` that returns the longest expression whose operators all bind **more strongly** than `power`:

```python fragment
def expression(self, power=LOWEST):
    left = self.prefix()                  # an operand, or a prefix operator and its operand
    while (the next token is an operator in INFIX, with a power greater than `power`):
        left = self.infix(left, that_power)   # it takes `left` as its left side
    return left
```

`prefix()` handles whatever can **start** an expression: a number, a string, `true`, `false`, `nil`, a name, a bracketed expression, a list or map literal, or a prefix operator. `infix(left, power)` handles an operator **after** an operand: it consumes the operator, parses what the operator needs on its right, and returns the new node.

Here is `1 + 2 * 3 - 4` step by step, starting from `expression(LOWEST)`:

| step | next token | its power | action | left |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | | | prefix reads `1` | `1` |
| 2 | `+` | 5 > 0 | infix `+`: its right side is `expression(5)` | |
| 3 | | | inside: prefix reads `2`; next is `*`, 6 > 5, so `*` takes `2` and reads `3`; next is `-`, 5 is not > 5, return `(* 2 3)` | |
| 4 | | | back out: `+` builds its node | `(+ 1 (* 2 3))` |
| 5 | `-` | 5 > 0 | infix `-`: right side `expression(5)` reads `4` and returns | `(- (+ 1 (* 2 3)) 4)` |
| 6 | end | | too weak: return | |

Step 3 is the whole trick. The right side of `+` is parsed with `+`'s own power, so it may only contain **stronger** operators. The `*` gets in; the `-`, equally strong, does not.

### Left to right, from one comparison

That same rule gives left associativity for free. In `10 - 3 - 2`, the right side of the first `-` is `expression(SUM)`, which reads `3` and stops at the second `-` because its power is not **greater** than `SUM`. So the first subtraction closes first: `(- (- 10 3) 2)`, which is 5, as it should be.

If the test were "greater than or equal", the second `-` would get into the right side, the tree would be `(- 10 (- 3 2))`, and the answer would be 9. One character decides associativity. A right-associative operator, such as a power operator where `2^3^2` means `2^(3^2)`, is made on purpose by parsing its right side with a power one lower than its own.

### Prefix operators

A prefix operator parses its operand with a chosen power:

- `-` in front parses `expression(UNARY)`. Only postfix operators are stronger, so `-f(x)` is `(- (call f x))` and `-2 * 3` is `(* (- 2) 3)`.
- `not` parses `expression(NOT)`. Comparisons and arithmetic are stronger, and `and` and `or` are weaker, so `not a == b and c` is `(and (not (== a b)) c)`. That matches the grammar rule `not = "not" not | compare`.

Both are handled in `prefix()`, and both call `expression` again, so `- -x` and `not not ok` work with no extra code.

### Calls, indexes and literals

A call or an index comes after a complete operand, so it is an entry in `INFIX` with the strongest power, `POSTFIX`. Its `infix` case is different from a binary operator's:

- After `(`, read comma-separated arguments up to `)`. The node is `Call(callee, args)`.
- After `[`, read one expression, then expect `]`. The node is `Index(target, index)`.

Because the loop keeps going while the next operator is strong enough, chains work by themselves: `f(1)(2)[0]` is a call, then a call on its result, then an index.

A list literal starts with `[` in prefix position: comma-separated items up to `]`. A map literal starts with `{`: comma-separated `key : value` pairs up to `}`. Keys are ordinary expressions; a later milestone checks that they turn out to be strings. The same `[` means two things, an index after an operand and a list at the start of one, and Pratt parsing separates them naturally: `prefix` sees one, `infix` the other.

### Where each node points

A node's position is where an error about it should point:

- a literal, a name, a list or a map: its first token;
- `Unary` and `Binary`: the operator's token, so "division by zero" will point at the `/`;
- `Index`: the `[`;
- `Call`: the **callee's** position, so "`f` expects 2 arguments" points at the `f`, not at a bracket.

### Comparisons do not chain

In Python, `1 < x < 9` means `1 < x and x < 9`. In C it means `(1 < x) < 9`, which compares a boolean with 9. Comet refuses both. After building a comparison, if the next token is also a comparison, raise the error `comparisons cannot be chained`, at that second operator.

### Errors

This milestone stops at the first syntax error by raising `ParseError(message, line, col)`, which is a `StaticError` like `LexError`. The next milestone adds recovery. The messages name what was expected and what was found. The starter's `describe(tok)` names a token: `'+'` for most tokens, `a string` for a string, and `end of input` for `EOF`. When `prefix` meets a token that cannot start an expression, the message is `expected an expression, found ` followed by that description, at that token. `expect(text)` makes `expected ')', found ';'`.

### Why it is correct, and why it stops

**It stops.** `prefix` always consumes at least one token or raises an error, and each pass of the loop consumes the operator. Tokens are finite, so the parser finishes.

**It builds the right tree.** The claim, proved by induction on the number of tokens it reads, is: `expression(p)` returns the tree of the longest expression starting here whose operators all have power greater than `p`, grouped by power and then left to right. Each pass of the loop joins the operand built so far with the next operator's right side, and that right side is, by the claim for fewer tokens, the longest stretch of stronger operators. So no weaker operator ends up inside a stronger one's operand, which is exactly what precedence means.

### What it costs

Each token is consumed once and every loop test is O(1), so parsing n tokens takes Θ(n) time. Memory is the tree, Θ(n), plus Python's recursion, which goes as deep as the expression's brackets and prefix operators nest. Deep nesting, such as a hundred opening brackets, can exhaust Python's stack, so real parsers either limit nesting or parse without recursion.

### How to test it

Print trees with `sexpr` and compare strings: `(+ 1 (* 2 3))`. One test per rule: each precedence level against its neighbours, associativity, each prefix operator, calls, indexes, chains, literals, and each error with its exact position. Compare whole trees built by hand, with `==`, to check the node classes and fields.

### Where it is used

- Vaughan Pratt published the method in 1973. [[It was rediscovered much later|pratt]]: JSLint used it, and so do rust-analyzer and the bytecode Lox interpreter of *Crafting Interpreters*.
- Clang and GCC parse C expressions with precedence climbing, which is the same idea arranged slightly differently.
- Anything with a formula bar, from spreadsheets to the ground-software tools where operators type limits like `temp > 40 and not safe_mode`, parses expressions like this.

**Watch out:** the bugs that make a Pratt parser quietly wrong.

- Testing `op_power >= power` instead of `>`. Everything parses, but `10 - 3 - 2` gives 9. Only a test of associativity catches it.
- Giving the operand of prefix `-` the power `LOWEST`, so `-1 + 2` becomes `-(1 + 2)`.
- Looking only at a token's text: a string token whose text is `or`, from the source `"or"`, is not the operator. Check the kind too.
- Forgetting to consume the operator in `infix` before parsing its right side, so the right side starts with the operator itself.

::: context kwonly Keyword-only dataclass fields
A dataclass normally needs fields with defaults to come after fields without them, so a base class with defaulted `line` and `col` would break every subclass that adds a plain field. Since Python 3.10, `kw_only=True` removes the problem: such fields are moved to the end of the generated `__init__` and must be given by name. `compare=False` leaves a field out of the generated `__eq__`, and `repr=False` out of the printed form, which keeps printed trees short.
:::

::: context sexp Prefix expressions
Writing the operator first and every group in brackets is how Lisp has written programs since 1958, where these are called S-expressions (symbolic expressions). They need no precedence rules at all, because the brackets show every grouping. That is exactly why they are useful in tests: `(- (- 10 3) 2)` says, in one short line, the thing a test of associativity needs to see, and two trees are equal exactly when their prefix forms are equal.
:::

::: context shunting The shunting-yard algorithm
Edsger Dijkstra described it in 1961, named after a railway yard where carriages are sorted onto side tracks. It reads tokens left to right, sends numbers straight to the output, and holds operators on a stack until a weaker operator arrives and pushes them out. The output is postfix (reverse Polish) notation, ready for a stack machine. Pratt parsing and shunting-yard make the same decisions: an operator on the stack is popped exactly when the Pratt loop would stop and return.
:::

::: context pratt Top-down operator precedence
Vaughan Pratt, who later worked on the Sun workstation and co-founded the company behind it, presented "Top Down Operator Precedence" in 1973. It sat mostly unused for decades while parser generators such as yacc were fashionable. Douglas Crockford's 2007 article on writing a JavaScript parser this way brought it back, and Bob Nystrom's writing and his book *Crafting Interpreters* made it common. Its appeal is that each operator carries its own parsing rule and strength, so adding an operator changes one place.
:::
--- task
The starter gives the node classes (including `Nil`, `Index`, `ListLit` and `MapLit`), `ParseError`, `describe`, the binding powers (`LOWEST` … `POSTFIX`, `COMPARISONS`, `INFIX`), a `Parser` with `peek()`, `at(*texts)`, `advance()`, `error(message, tok=None)` and `expect(text)`, the function `parse_expression(source)`, and the helpers `quote` and `group`. Write:

- `Parser.expression(power=LOWEST)`: the Pratt loop, with any helpers you like (for example `prefix()` and `infix(left, power)`). It parses:
  - numbers (`Num` with an int), strings (`Str`), `true` and `false` (`Bool`), `nil` (`Nil`), names (`Var`), and a bracketed expression (the inner node, with no node for the brackets);
  - prefix `-` with operand power `UNARY` and prefix `not` with operand power `NOT`, as `Unary(op, expr)`;
  - the binary operators of `INFIX`, left to right, as `Binary(op, left, right)`; after a comparison, if the next token is another comparison, raise `ParseError` `comparisons cannot be chained` at that token;
  - calls `Call(callee, args)` and indexes `Index(target, index)`, which can chain;
  - list literals `ListLit(items)` and map literals `MapLit(pairs)` with `pairs` a list of `(key, value)` tuples; `[]` and `{}` are empty ones.
  - Positions: a literal, name, list or map at its first token; `Unary`, `Binary` at the operator; `Index` at the `[`; `Call` at the callee's position.
  - A token that cannot start an expression raises `ParseError` `expected an expression, found X` at it, where X is `describe(token)`. Missing brackets, commas and colons raise the error from `expect`.
- `sexpr(node)`: the prefix form. Numbers as digits, strings with `quote`, `true`, `false`, `nil`, a name as itself, `(op operand…)` for `Unary` and `Binary`, `(call callee arg…)`, `(index target index)`, `(list item…)`, and `(map key value key value…)`. For example `sexpr(parse_expression('f(1)[0] + -x'))` is `(+ (index (call f 1) 0) (- x))`.
--- starter
"""Comet: a small programming language, built in layers.

    source text -> Lexer -> tokens -> Parser -> syntax tree
                -> Resolver -> Interpreter -> printed output

Each layer only talks to the one after it, so each can be tested alone.
"""
import operator
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


# ============================================================================
# Tokens and the lexer
# ============================================================================

KEYWORDS = {
    "let", "fn", "return", "if", "else", "while", "for", "in", "break",
    "continue", "print", "true", "false", "nil", "and", "or", "not",
}
TWO_CHAR = {"==", "!=", "<=", ">=", "->"}
ONE_CHAR = set("+-*/%<>=(){}[],;:")
ESCAPES = {'"': '"', "\\": "\\", "n": "\n"}
DIGITS = set("0123456789")
LETTERS = set("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ_")
# Characters people type from other languages, and what Comet wants instead.
LEX_HINTS = {
    "'": "strings use double quotes",
    "&": "use 'and'",
    "|": "use 'or'",
    "!": "use 'not', or '!=' for not equal",
}


@dataclass
class Token:
    kind: str   # NUMBER, STRING, IDENT, KEYWORD, OP or EOF
    text: str   # the source text; for a STRING, the decoded value
    line: int   # counted from 1
    col: int    # counted from 1


class StaticError(Exception):
    """A mistake found before the program runs. Prints as "line:col: message"."""

    def __init__(self, message, line, col):
        super().__init__(f"{line}:{col}: {message}")
        self.message = message
        self.line = line
        self.col = col


class LexError(StaticError):
    """A character sequence that is not a Comet token."""


class Lexer:
    """Turns source text into tokens. It keeps going after a mistake, so one
    scan reports every lexing error, each with its line and column."""

    def __init__(self, source):
        self.source = source
        self.pos = 0          # index of the next character to read
        self.line = 1         # where that character is, for messages
        self.col = 1
        self.tokens = []
        self.errors = []

    def peek(self, ahead=0):
        """A character ahead of the read position, or "" past the end."""
        i = self.pos + ahead
        return self.source[i] if i < len(self.source) else ""

    def advance(self):
        """Consumes one character and keeps line and col in step with it."""
        ch = self.source[self.pos]
        self.pos += 1
        if ch == "\n":
            self.line += 1
            self.col = 1
        else:
            self.col += 1
        return ch

    def scan(self):
        """Returns (tokens, errors): every token ending with EOF, and every LexError."""
        while self.pos < len(self.source):
            self.scan_token()
        self.tokens.append(Token("EOF", "", self.line, self.col))
        return self.tokens, self.errors

    def scan_token(self):
        line, col = self.line, self.col
        ch = self.peek()
        if ch in " \t\r\n":
            self.advance()
        elif ch == "#":
            while self.peek() not in ("", "\n"):
                self.advance()
        elif ch in DIGITS:
            self.number(line, col)
        elif ch in LETTERS:
            self.word(line, col)
        elif ch == '"':
            self.string(line, col)
        elif ch + self.peek(1) in TWO_CHAR:
            text = self.advance() + self.advance()
            self.tokens.append(Token("OP", text, line, col))
        elif ch in ONE_CHAR:
            self.tokens.append(Token("OP", self.advance(), line, col))
        else:
            self.advance()   # skip it, report it, and carry on
            message = f"unexpected character {ch!r}"
            if ch in LEX_HINTS:
                message += f" ({LEX_HINTS[ch]})"
            self.errors.append(LexError(message, line, col))

    def number(self, line, col):
        start = self.pos
        while self.peek() in DIGITS:
            self.advance()
        self.tokens.append(Token("NUMBER", self.source[start:self.pos], line, col))

    def word(self, line, col):
        start = self.pos
        while self.peek() in LETTERS or self.peek() in DIGITS:
            self.advance()
        text = self.source[start:self.pos]
        kind = "KEYWORD" if text in KEYWORDS else "IDENT"
        self.tokens.append(Token(kind, text, line, col))

    def string(self, line, col):
        """A string literal. The token's text is the decoded value."""
        self.advance()  # the opening quote
        chars = []
        while True:
            ch = self.peek()
            if ch in ("", "\n"):
                # Strings never span lines, so the rest of this line is lost.
                self.errors.append(LexError("unterminated string", line, col))
                return
            if ch == '"':
                self.advance()
                break
            if ch == "\\":
                at_line, at_col = self.line, self.col
                self.advance()
                code = self.peek()
                if code in ESCAPES:
                    chars.append(ESCAPES[self.advance()])
                elif code not in ("", "\n"):
                    self.advance()
                    self.errors.append(LexError(f"unknown escape \\{code}", at_line, at_col))
                continue
            chars.append(self.advance())
        self.tokens.append(Token("STRING", "".join(chars), line, col))


def tokenize(source):
    """The tokens of source; raises the first LexError if there is one."""
    tokens, errors = Lexer(source).scan()
    if errors:
        raise errors[0]
    return tokens


def point_at(source, line, col):
    """Two lines: source line `line`, and a caret under column `col`.
    Tabs before the column are copied, so the caret lines up in a terminal."""
    lines = source.split("\n")
    text = lines[line - 1] if 1 <= line <= len(lines) else ""
    pad = "".join("\t" if c == "\t" else " " for c in text[:col - 1])
    return text + "\n" + pad.ljust(col - 1) + "^"


# ============================================================================
# The syntax tree
# ============================================================================

def pos_field():
    """A node's line or column: given by keyword, and never part of ==."""
    return field(default=0, kw_only=True, compare=False, repr=False)


@dataclass
class Node:
    line: int = pos_field()
    col: int = pos_field()


@dataclass
class Num(Node):
    value: int


@dataclass
class Str(Node):
    value: str


@dataclass
class Bool(Node):
    value: bool


@dataclass
class Nil(Node):
    pass


@dataclass
class Var(Node):
    name: str


@dataclass
class Unary(Node):
    op: str
    expr: Node


@dataclass
class Binary(Node):
    op: str
    left: Node
    right: Node


@dataclass
class Call(Node):
    callee: Node
    args: list


@dataclass
class Index(Node):
    target: Node
    index: Node


@dataclass
class ListLit(Node):
    items: list


@dataclass
class MapLit(Node):
    pairs: list     # (key, value) pairs of expressions


# ============================================================================
# The parser
# ============================================================================

class ParseError(StaticError):
    """Tokens in an order the grammar does not allow."""


def describe(tok):
    """How a token is named in an error message."""
    if tok.kind == "EOF":
        return "end of input"
    if tok.kind == "STRING":
        return "a string"
    return f"'{tok.text}'"


# Binding powers, weakest first. An operator with a higher power takes its
# operands before an operator with a lower power does.
LOWEST, OR, AND, NOT, COMPARE, SUM, PRODUCT, UNARY, POSTFIX = range(9)
COMPARISONS = ("==", "!=", "<", "<=", ">", ">=")
INFIX = {
    "or": OR, "and": AND,
    "==": COMPARE, "!=": COMPARE, "<": COMPARE, "<=": COMPARE, ">": COMPARE, ">=": COMPARE,
    "+": SUM, "-": SUM,
    "*": PRODUCT, "/": PRODUCT, "%": PRODUCT,
    "(": POSTFIX, "[": POSTFIX,
}


class Parser:
    """A Pratt parser for expressions, and recursive descent for statements."""

    def __init__(self, tokens):
        self.tokens = tokens
        self.pos = 0

    def peek(self):
        return self.tokens[self.pos]

    def at(self, *texts):
        """Is the next token one of these operators or keywords?"""
        tok = self.tokens[self.pos]
        return tok.kind in ("OP", "KEYWORD") and tok.text in texts

    def advance(self):
        """Consumes the next token and returns it. EOF is never consumed."""
        tok = self.tokens[self.pos]
        if tok.kind != "EOF":
            self.pos += 1
        return tok

    def error(self, message, tok=None):
        tok = tok or self.peek()
        return ParseError(message, tok.line, tok.col)

    def expect(self, text):
        if not self.at(text):
            raise self.error(f"expected '{text}', found {describe(self.peek())}")
        return self.advance()

    def expression(self, power=LOWEST):
        """An expression whose operators all bind more tightly than `power`."""
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 2: Parser.expression")


def parse_expression(source):
    """One expression and nothing after it. Raises the first LexError or ParseError."""
    parser = Parser(tokenize(source))
    expr = parser.expression()
    if parser.peek().kind != "EOF":
        raise parser.error(f"expected end of input, found {describe(parser.peek())}")
    return expr


def quote(text):
    """A string as Comet source writes it: in quotes, with its escapes."""
    return '"' + text.replace("\\", "\\\\").replace('"', '\\"').replace("\n", "\\n") + '"'


def group(head, *parts):
    return "(" + " ".join([head, *parts]) + ")"


def sexpr(node):
    """The tree as a prefix expression: 1 + 2 * x becomes (+ 1 (* 2 x))."""
    raise NotImplementedError("milestone 2: sexpr")
--- solution
"""Comet: a small programming language, built in layers.

    source text -> Lexer -> tokens -> Parser -> syntax tree
                -> Resolver -> Interpreter -> printed output

Each layer only talks to the one after it, so each can be tested alone.
"""
import operator
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


# ============================================================================
# Tokens and the lexer
# ============================================================================

KEYWORDS = {
    "let", "fn", "return", "if", "else", "while", "for", "in", "break",
    "continue", "print", "true", "false", "nil", "and", "or", "not",
}
TWO_CHAR = {"==", "!=", "<=", ">=", "->"}
ONE_CHAR = set("+-*/%<>=(){}[],;:")
ESCAPES = {'"': '"', "\\": "\\", "n": "\n"}
DIGITS = set("0123456789")
LETTERS = set("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ_")
# Characters people type from other languages, and what Comet wants instead.
LEX_HINTS = {
    "'": "strings use double quotes",
    "&": "use 'and'",
    "|": "use 'or'",
    "!": "use 'not', or '!=' for not equal",
}


@dataclass
class Token:
    kind: str   # NUMBER, STRING, IDENT, KEYWORD, OP or EOF
    text: str   # the source text; for a STRING, the decoded value
    line: int   # counted from 1
    col: int    # counted from 1


class StaticError(Exception):
    """A mistake found before the program runs. Prints as "line:col: message"."""

    def __init__(self, message, line, col):
        super().__init__(f"{line}:{col}: {message}")
        self.message = message
        self.line = line
        self.col = col


class LexError(StaticError):
    """A character sequence that is not a Comet token."""


class Lexer:
    """Turns source text into tokens. It keeps going after a mistake, so one
    scan reports every lexing error, each with its line and column."""

    def __init__(self, source):
        self.source = source
        self.pos = 0          # index of the next character to read
        self.line = 1         # where that character is, for messages
        self.col = 1
        self.tokens = []
        self.errors = []

    def peek(self, ahead=0):
        """A character ahead of the read position, or "" past the end."""
        i = self.pos + ahead
        return self.source[i] if i < len(self.source) else ""

    def advance(self):
        """Consumes one character and keeps line and col in step with it."""
        ch = self.source[self.pos]
        self.pos += 1
        if ch == "\n":
            self.line += 1
            self.col = 1
        else:
            self.col += 1
        return ch

    def scan(self):
        """Returns (tokens, errors): every token ending with EOF, and every LexError."""
        while self.pos < len(self.source):
            self.scan_token()
        self.tokens.append(Token("EOF", "", self.line, self.col))
        return self.tokens, self.errors

    def scan_token(self):
        line, col = self.line, self.col
        ch = self.peek()
        if ch in " \t\r\n":
            self.advance()
        elif ch == "#":
            while self.peek() not in ("", "\n"):
                self.advance()
        elif ch in DIGITS:
            self.number(line, col)
        elif ch in LETTERS:
            self.word(line, col)
        elif ch == '"':
            self.string(line, col)
        elif ch + self.peek(1) in TWO_CHAR:
            text = self.advance() + self.advance()
            self.tokens.append(Token("OP", text, line, col))
        elif ch in ONE_CHAR:
            self.tokens.append(Token("OP", self.advance(), line, col))
        else:
            self.advance()   # skip it, report it, and carry on
            message = f"unexpected character {ch!r}"
            if ch in LEX_HINTS:
                message += f" ({LEX_HINTS[ch]})"
            self.errors.append(LexError(message, line, col))

    def number(self, line, col):
        start = self.pos
        while self.peek() in DIGITS:
            self.advance()
        self.tokens.append(Token("NUMBER", self.source[start:self.pos], line, col))

    def word(self, line, col):
        start = self.pos
        while self.peek() in LETTERS or self.peek() in DIGITS:
            self.advance()
        text = self.source[start:self.pos]
        kind = "KEYWORD" if text in KEYWORDS else "IDENT"
        self.tokens.append(Token(kind, text, line, col))

    def string(self, line, col):
        """A string literal. The token's text is the decoded value."""
        self.advance()  # the opening quote
        chars = []
        while True:
            ch = self.peek()
            if ch in ("", "\n"):
                # Strings never span lines, so the rest of this line is lost.
                self.errors.append(LexError("unterminated string", line, col))
                return
            if ch == '"':
                self.advance()
                break
            if ch == "\\":
                at_line, at_col = self.line, self.col
                self.advance()
                code = self.peek()
                if code in ESCAPES:
                    chars.append(ESCAPES[self.advance()])
                elif code not in ("", "\n"):
                    self.advance()
                    self.errors.append(LexError(f"unknown escape \\{code}", at_line, at_col))
                continue
            chars.append(self.advance())
        self.tokens.append(Token("STRING", "".join(chars), line, col))


def tokenize(source):
    """The tokens of source; raises the first LexError if there is one."""
    tokens, errors = Lexer(source).scan()
    if errors:
        raise errors[0]
    return tokens


def point_at(source, line, col):
    """Two lines: source line `line`, and a caret under column `col`.
    Tabs before the column are copied, so the caret lines up in a terminal."""
    lines = source.split("\n")
    text = lines[line - 1] if 1 <= line <= len(lines) else ""
    pad = "".join("\t" if c == "\t" else " " for c in text[:col - 1])
    return text + "\n" + pad.ljust(col - 1) + "^"

    """A node's line or column: given by keyword, and never part of ==."""
    return field(default=0, kw_only=True, compare=False, repr=False)


@dataclass
class Node:
    line: int = pos_field()
    col: int = pos_field()


@dataclass
class Num(Node):
    value: int


@dataclass
class Str(Node):
    value: str


@dataclass
class Bool(Node):
    value: bool


@dataclass
class Nil(Node):
    pass


@dataclass
class Var(Node):
    name: str

class Unary(Node):
    op: str
    expr: Node
