# The resolver: names and jumps, checked before anything runs
# ============================================================================

class ResolveError(StaticError):
    """A name or a jump used where it cannot be."""


class Resolver:
    """Checks names and jumps before the program runs, and records on each
    Var and Assign how many scopes out the declaration is (None: a global)."""

    def __init__(self):
        raise NotImplementedError("milestone 6: Resolver")


def resolve(program):
    """Resolves every name in program; returns the list of ResolveErrors."""
    raise NotImplementedError("milestone 6: resolve")


# ============================================================================
# Values
# ============================================================================

class CometError(Exception):
    """A runtime error in the Comet program (not a bug in the interpreter)."""


def comet_div(a, b):
    """Integer division that rounds toward zero, like C."""
    if b == 0:
        raise CometError("division by zero")
    q = abs(a) // abs(b)
    return q if (a < 0) == (b < 0) else -q


def comet_mod(a, b):
    return a - b * comet_div(a, b)


def type_name(value):
    """Comet's name for a value's type."""
    if value is None:
        return "nil"
    if isinstance(value, bool):     # before int: in Python, True is an int
        return "bool"
    if isinstance(value, int):
        return "int"
    if isinstance(value, str):
        return "str"
    if isinstance(value, Closure):
        return "fn"
    raise TypeError(f"not a Comet value: {value!r}")


def repr_value(value):
    """A value as Comet source writes it: strings in quotes."""
    if value is None:
        return "nil"
    if isinstance(value, bool):
        return "true" if value else "false"
    if isinstance(value, int):
        return str(value)
    if isinstance(value, str):
        return quote(value)
    if isinstance(value, Closure):
        return f"<fn {value.name}>" if value.name else "<fn>"
    raise TypeError(f"not a Comet value: {value!r}")


def show(value):
    """What print writes: a string as it is, anything else as repr_value."""
    return value if isinstance(value, str) else repr_value(value)


def values_equal(a, b):
    """Comet's ==: values of different types are never equal."""
    if type_name(a) != type_name(b):
        return False
    return a == b    # same Comet type, so Python's == is right (fns: the same fn)


ARITHMETIC = {
    "+": operator.add, "-": operator.sub, "*": operator.mul, "/": comet_div, "%": comet_mod,
    "<": operator.lt, "<=": operator.le, ">": operator.gt, ">=": operator.ge,
}
ORDERING = ("<", "<=", ">", ">=")
JOINABLE = ("str",)             # + also joins two of these


def arithmetic(op, left, right):
    """+ - * / % < <= > >= with Comet's type rules."""
    lt, rt = type_name(left), type_name(right)
    if lt == rt == "int":
        return ARITHMETIC[op](left, right)
    if op == "+" and lt == rt and lt in JOINABLE:
        return left + right
    if op in ORDERING and lt == rt == "str":
        return ARITHMETIC[op](left, right)
    raise CometError(f"'{op}' cannot combine {lt} and {rt}")


class Closure:
    """A Comet function value: its declaration (an Fn or FnExpr node) and
    the Environment it was made in, which it keeps alive."""

    def __init__(self, decl, env):
        self.decl = decl
        self.env = env

    @property
    def name(self):
        return self.decl.name if isinstance(self.decl, Fn) else None

    def label(self):
        return self.name or "anonymous fn"


class ReturnSignal(Exception):
    """Carries a return value up to the call waiting for it. Not a
    CometError, so nothing a Comet program does can catch it."""

    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value


def check_arity(name, fewest, most, got):
    if fewest <= got <= most:
        return
    if fewest == most:
        wanted = f"{fewest} argument" + ("" if fewest == 1 else "s")
    elif most == fewest + 1:
        wanted = f"{fewest} or {most} arguments"
    else:
        wanted = f"{fewest} to {most} arguments"
    raise CometError(f"{name} expects {wanted}, got {got}")


# ============================================================================
# The interpreter
# ============================================================================


class Environment:
    """One scope's variables, and the scope around it (None for the globals)."""

    def __init__(self, parent=None):
        self.values = {}
        self.parent = parent

    def define(self, name, value):
        if self.parent is not None and name in self.values:
            raise CometError(f"{name} is already declared in this scope")
        self.values[name] = value

    def lookup(self, name):
        env = self
        while env is not None:
            if name in env.values:
                return env.values[name]
            env = env.parent
        raise CometError(f"undefined variable {name}")

    def assign(self, name, value):
        env = self
        while env is not None:
            if name in env.values:
                env.values[name] = value
                return
            env = env.parent
        raise CometError(f"assignment to undeclared variable {name}")


class Interpreter:
    """Runs a syntax tree. Printed lines collect in self.output."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.globals = Environment()
        self.env = self.globals       # the scope running now
        self.output = []

    def run(self, program):
        for stmt in program.stmts:
            try:
                self.execute(stmt)
            except ReturnSignal:
                raise CometError("return outside a function") from None

    def handler(self, prefix, node):
        """The method for this kind of node: exec_Print for a Print, and so on."""
        method = getattr(self, prefix + type(node).__name__, None)
        if method is None:
            raise CometError(f"{type(node).__name__} is not supported yet")
        return method

    def execute(self, stmt):
        self.handler("exec_", stmt)(stmt)

    def evaluate(self, expr):
        return self.handler("eval_", expr)(expr)

    def execute_block(self, stmts, env):
        """Runs stmts with env as the current scope, and always puts the old
        scope back, also when a statement raises."""
        previous = self.env
        self.env = env
        try:
            for stmt in stmts:
                self.execute(stmt)
        finally:
            self.env = previous

    # ---- statements ----

    def exec_Let(self, stmt):
        self.env.define(stmt.name, self.evaluate(stmt.expr))

    def exec_Assign(self, stmt):
        value = self.evaluate(stmt.expr)
        self.env.assign(stmt.name, value)

    def exec_Print(self, stmt):
        self.output.append(show(self.evaluate(stmt.expr)))

    def exec_ExprStmt(self, stmt):
        self.evaluate(stmt.expr)

    def exec_If(self, stmt):
        if self.condition(stmt.cond):
            self.execute(stmt.then)
        elif stmt.else_ is not None:
            self.execute(stmt.else_)    # a Block, or an If for "else if"

    def exec_While(self, stmt):
        while self.condition(stmt.cond):
            self.execute(stmt.body)

    def exec_Block(self, stmt):
        self.execute_block(stmt.stmts, Environment(self.env))

    def condition(self, expr):
        value = self.evaluate(expr)
        if not isinstance(value, bool):
            raise CometError(f"a condition must be bool, not {type_name(value)}")
        return value

    # ---- expressions ----

    def eval_Num(self, expr):
        return expr.value

    eval_Str = eval_Bool = eval_Num

    def eval_Nil(self, expr):
        return None

    def eval_Var(self, expr):
        return self.env.lookup(expr.name)

    def eval_Unary(self, expr):
        value = self.evaluate(expr.expr)
        if expr.op == "-":
            self.need("int", value, "-")
            return -value
        self.need("bool", value, "not")
        return not value

    def need(self, wanted, value, op):
        if type_name(value) != wanted:
            raise CometError(f"'{op}' needs {wanted}, not {type_name(value)}")

    def eval_Binary(self, expr):
        op = expr.op
        left = self.evaluate(expr.left)
        if op in ("and", "or"):
            self.need("bool", left, op)
            if left == (op == "or"):     # false and ..., true or ...: already decided
                return left
            right = self.evaluate(expr.right)
            self.need("bool", right, op)
            return right
        right = self.evaluate(expr.right)
        if op in ("==", "!="):
            lt, rt = type_name(left), type_name(right)
            if lt != rt and "nil" not in (lt, rt):
                raise CometError(f"cannot compare {lt} with {rt}")
            return values_equal(left, right) == (op == "==")
        return arithmetic(op, left, right)

    # ---- functions ----

    def exec_Fn(self, stmt):
        self.env.define(stmt.name, Closure(stmt, self.env))

    def eval_FnExpr(self, expr):
        return Closure(expr, self.env)

    def exec_Return(self, stmt):
        value = None if stmt.expr is None else self.evaluate(stmt.expr)
        raise ReturnSignal(value)

    def eval_Call(self, expr):
        callee = self.evaluate(expr.callee)
        args = [self.evaluate(arg) for arg in expr.args]
        return self.call(callee, args)

    def call(self, callee, args):
        """Calls a function value with argument values, and returns its result."""
        if isinstance(callee, Closure):
            params = callee.decl.params
            check_arity(callee.label(), len(params), len(params), len(args))
            env = Environment(callee.env)   # inside the fn's own scope, not the caller's
            for (name, _type), value in zip(params, args):
                env.define(name, value)
            try:
                self.execute_block(callee.decl.body.stmts, env)
            except ReturnSignal as signal:
                return signal.value
            return None
        raise CometError(f"cannot call a value of type {type_name(callee)}")


def run(source):
    """Runs a Comet program and returns what it printed, one line per print.
    Errors found before running are the whole answer; a runtime error is
    added after whatever was printed before it."""
    program, errors = parse(source)
    if errors:
        return "\n".join(str(e) for e in errors)
    interp = Interpreter()
    try:
        interp.run(program)
    except CometError as e:
        interp.output.append(f"runtime error: {e}")
    return "\n".join(interp.output)
--- solution
"""Comet: a small programming language, built in layers.

    source text -> Lexer -> tokens -> Parser -> syntax tree
                -> Resolver -> Interpreter -> printed output

Each layer only talks to the one after it, so each can be tested alone.
"""
import operator
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


# ============================================================================
# Tokens and the lexer
# ============================================================================

KEYWORDS = {
    "let", "fn", "return", "if", "else", "while", "for", "in", "break",
    "continue", "print", "true", "false", "nil", "and", "or", "not",
}
TWO_CHAR = {"==", "!=", "<=", ">=", "->"}
ONE_CHAR = set("+-*/%<>=(){}[],;:")
ESCAPES = {'"': '"', "\\": "\\", "n": "\n"}
DIGITS = set("0123456789")
LETTERS = set("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ_")
# Characters people type from other languages, and what Comet wants instead.
LEX_HINTS = {
    "'": "strings use double quotes",
    "&": "use 'and'",
    "|": "use 'or'",
    "!": "use 'not', or '!=' for not equal",
}


@dataclass
class Token:
    kind: str   # NUMBER, STRING, IDENT, KEYWORD, OP or EOF
    text: str   # the source text; for a STRING, the decoded value
    line: int   # counted from 1
    col: int    # counted from 1


class StaticError(Exception):
    """A mistake found before the program runs. Prints as "line:col: message"."""

    def __init__(self, message, line, col):
        super().__init__(f"{line}:{col}: {message}")
        self.message = message
        self.line = line
        self.col = col


class LexError(StaticError):
    """A character sequence that is not a Comet token."""


class Lexer:
    """Turns source text into tokens. It keeps going after a mistake, so one
    scan reports every lexing error, each with its line and column."""

    def __init__(self, source):
        self.source = source
        self.pos = 0          # index of the next character to read
        self.line = 1         # where that character is, for messages
        self.col = 1
        self.tokens = []
        self.errors = []

    def peek(self, ahead=0):
        """A character ahead of the read position, or "" past the end."""
        i = self.pos + ahead
        return self.source[i] if i < len(self.source) else ""

    def advance(self):
        """Consumes one character and keeps line and col in step with it."""
        ch = self.source[self.pos]
        self.pos += 1
        if ch == "\n":
            self.line += 1
            self.col = 1
        else:
            self.col += 1
        return ch

    def scan(self):
        """Returns (tokens, errors): every token ending with EOF, and every LexError."""
        while self.pos < len(self.source):
            self.scan_token()
        self.tokens.append(Token("EOF", "", self.line, self.col))
        return self.tokens, self.errors

    def scan_token(self):
        line, col = self.line, self.col
        ch = self.peek()
        if ch in " \t\r\n":
            self.advance()
        elif ch == "#":
            while self.peek() not in ("", "\n"):
                self.advance()
        elif ch in DIGITS:
            self.number(line, col)
        elif ch in LETTERS:
            self.word(line, col)
        elif ch == '"':
            self.string(line, col)
        elif ch + self.peek(1) in TWO_CHAR:
            text = self.advance() + self.advance()
            self.tokens.append(Token("OP", text, line, col))
        elif ch in ONE_CHAR:
            self.tokens.append(Token("OP", self.advance(), line, col))
        else:
            self.advance()   # skip it, report it, and carry on
            message = f"unexpected character {ch!r}"
            if ch in LEX_HINTS:
                message += f" ({LEX_HINTS[ch]})"
            self.errors.append(LexError(message, line, col))

    def number(self, line, col):
        start = self.pos
        while self.peek() in DIGITS:
            self.advance()
        self.tokens.append(Token("NUMBER", self.source[start:self.pos], line, col))

    def word(self, line, col):
        start = self.pos
        while self.peek() in LETTERS or self.peek() in DIGITS:
            self.advance()
        text = self.source[start:self.pos]
        kind = "KEYWORD" if text in KEYWORDS else "IDENT"
        self.tokens.append(Token(kind, text, line, col))

    def string(self, line, col):
        """A string literal. The token's text is the decoded value."""
        self.advance()  # the opening quote
        chars = []
        while True:
            ch = self.peek()
            if ch in ("", "\n"):
                # Strings never span lines, so the rest of this line is lost.
                self.errors.append(LexError("unterminated string", line, col))
                return
            if ch == '"':
                self.advance()
                break
            if ch == "\\":
                at_line, at_col = self.line, self.col
                self.advance()
                code = self.peek()
                if code in ESCAPES:
                    chars.append(ESCAPES[self.advance()])
                elif code not in ("", "\n"):
                    self.advance()
                    self.errors.append(LexError(f"unknown escape \\{code}", at_line, at_col))
                continue
            chars.append(self.advance())
        self.tokens.append(Token("STRING", "".join(chars), line, col))


def tokenize(source):
    """The tokens of source; raises the first LexError if there is one."""
    tokens, errors = Lexer(source).scan()
    if errors:
        raise errors[0]
    return tokens


def point_at(source, line, col):
    """Two lines: source line `line`, and a caret under column `col`.
    Tabs before the column are copied, so the caret lines up in a terminal."""
    lines = source.split("\n")
    text = lines[line - 1] if 1 <= line <= len(lines) else ""
    pad = "".join("\t" if c == "\t" else " " for c in text[:col - 1])
    return text + "\n" + pad.ljust(col - 1) + "^"


# ============================================================================
# The syntax tree
# ============================================================================

def pos_field():
    """A node's line or column: given by keyword, and never part of ==."""
    return field(default=0, kw_only=True, compare=False, repr=False)


@dataclass
class Node:
    line: int = pos_field()
    col: int = pos_field()


@dataclass
class Num(Node):
    value: int


@dataclass
class Str(Node):
    value: str


@dataclass
class Bool(Node):
    value: bool


@dataclass
class Nil(Node):
    pass


@dataclass
class Var(Node):
    name: str
    # How many scopes out the declaration is, or None for a global.
    # Filled in by the resolver.
    depth: object = field(default=None, kw_only=True, compare=False, repr=False)


@dataclass
class Unary(Node):
    op: str
    expr: Node


@dataclass
class Binary(Node):
    op: str
    left: Node
    right: Node


@dataclass
class Call(Node):
    callee: Node
    args: list


@dataclass
class Index(Node):
    target: Node
    index: Node


@dataclass
class ListLit(Node):
    items: list


@dataclass
class MapLit(Node):
    pairs: list     # (key, value) pairs of expressions


@dataclass
class FnExpr(Node):
    params: list    # (name, type) pairs; type is None without an annotation
    ret: object
    body: object    # a Block


@dataclass
class Let(Node):
    name: str
    type: object
    expr: Node


@dataclass
class Assign(Node):
    name: str
    expr: Node
    depth: object = field(default=None, kw_only=True, compare=False, repr=False)


@dataclass
class SetIndex(Node):
    target: Node
    index: Node
    expr: Node


@dataclass
class Print(Node):
    expr: Node


@dataclass
class If(Node):
    cond: Node
    then: object
    else_: object   # None, a Block, or an If (for "else if")


@dataclass
class While(Node):
    cond: Node
    body: object


@dataclass
class For(Node):
    name: str
    iterable: Node
    body: object


@dataclass
class Break(Node):
    pass


@dataclass
class Continue(Node):
    pass


@dataclass
class Fn(Node):
    name: str
    params: list
    ret: object
    body: object


@dataclass
class Return(Node):
    expr: object    # None for a bare "return;"


@dataclass
class ExprStmt(Node):
    expr: Node


@dataclass
class Block(Node):
    stmts: list


@dataclass
class Program(Node):
    stmts: list


# ============================================================================
# The parser
# ============================================================================

class ParseError(StaticError):
    """Tokens in an order the grammar does not allow."""


def describe(tok):
    """How a token is named in an error message."""
    if tok.kind == "EOF":
        return "end of input"
    if tok.kind == "STRING":
        return "a string"
    return f"'{tok.text}'"


# Binding powers, weakest first. An operator with a higher power takes its
# operands before an operator with a lower power does.
LOWEST, OR, AND, NOT, COMPARE, SUM, PRODUCT, UNARY, POSTFIX = range(9)
COMPARISONS = ("==", "!=", "<", "<=", ">", ">=")
INFIX = {
    "or": OR, "and": AND,
    "==": COMPARE, "!=": COMPARE, "<": COMPARE, "<=": COMPARE, ">": COMPARE, ">=": COMPARE,
    "+": SUM, "-": SUM,
    "*": PRODUCT, "/": PRODUCT, "%": PRODUCT,
    "(": POSTFIX, "[": POSTFIX,
}
STATEMENT_START = ("let", "fn", "if", "while", "for", "return", "print", "break", "continue")
TYPES = ("int", "bool", "str", "list", "map", "any")


class Parser:
    """A Pratt parser for expressions, and recursive descent for statements."""

    def __init__(self, tokens):
        self.tokens = tokens
        self.pos = 0
        self.errors = []      # every ParseError found so far

    def peek(self):
        return self.tokens[self.pos]

    def at(self, *texts):
        """Is the next token one of these operators or keywords?"""
        tok = self.tokens[self.pos]
        return tok.kind in ("OP", "KEYWORD") and tok.text in texts

    def advance(self):
        """Consumes the next token and returns it. EOF is never consumed."""
        tok = self.tokens[self.pos]
        if tok.kind != "EOF":
            self.pos += 1
        return tok

    def error(self, message, tok=None):
        tok = tok or self.peek()
        return ParseError(message, tok.line, tok.col)

    def expect(self, text):
        if not self.at(text):
            raise self.error(f"expected '{text}', found {describe(self.peek())}")
        return self.advance()

    # ---- expressions: the Pratt loop -------------------------------------

    def expression(self, power=LOWEST):
        """An expression whose operators all bind more tightly than `power`."""
        left = self.prefix()
        while True:
            tok = self.peek()
            op_power = INFIX.get(tok.text, LOWEST) if tok.kind in ("OP", "KEYWORD") else LOWEST
            if op_power <= power:
                return left
            left = self.infix(left, op_power)

    def prefix(self):
        """Something that can start an expression."""
        tok = self.peek()
        where = dict(line=tok.line, col=tok.col)
        if tok.kind == "NUMBER":
            self.advance()
            return Num(int(tok.text), **where)
        if tok.kind == "STRING":
            self.advance()
            return Str(tok.text, **where)
        if tok.kind == "IDENT":
            self.advance()
            return Var(tok.text, **where)
        if self.at("true", "false"):
            self.advance()
            return Bool(tok.text == "true", **where)
        if self.at("nil"):
            self.advance()
            return Nil(**where)
        if self.at("-", "not"):
            self.advance()
            operand = self.expression(UNARY if tok.text == "-" else NOT)
            return Unary(tok.text, operand, **where)
        if self.at("("):
            self.advance()
            inner = self.expression()
            self.expect(")")
            return inner
        if self.at("["):
            self.advance()
            return ListLit(self.items("]"), **where)
        if self.at("{"):
            self.advance()
            return MapLit(self.pairs(), **where)
        if self.at("fn"):
            return self.function_expr()
        raise self.error(f"expected an expression, found {describe(tok)}")

    def infix(self, left, power):
        """An operator after a complete left operand, and what it needs after it."""
        tok = self.advance()
        where = dict(line=tok.line, col=tok.col)
        if tok.text == "(":
            return Call(left, self.items(")"), line=left.line, col=left.col)
        if tok.text == "[":
            index = self.expression()
            self.expect("]")
            return Index(left, index, **where)
        # A binary operator. The right side may only hold operators that bind
        # more tightly, so a second operator of the same power ends it: that
        # is what makes 10 - 3 - 2 group as (10 - 3) - 2.
        node = Binary(tok.text, left, self.expression(power), **where)
        if tok.text in COMPARISONS and self.at(*COMPARISONS):
            raise self.error("comparisons cannot be chained")
        return node

    def items(self, close):
        """Comma-separated expressions up to `close`, which is consumed."""
        items = []
        if not self.at(close):
            items.append(self.expression())
            while self.at(","):
                self.advance()
                items.append(self.expression())
        self.expect(close)
        return items

    def pairs(self):
        """The key: value pairs of a map literal, up to and including '}'."""
        pairs = []
        if not self.at("}"):
            pairs.append(self.pair())
            while self.at(","):
                self.advance()
                pairs.append(self.pair())
        self.expect("}")
        return pairs

    def pair(self):
        key = self.expression()
        self.expect(":")
        return (key, self.expression())

    # ---- statements, with error recovery ---------------------------------

    def program(self):
        """Every statement up to EOF. Errors are collected in self.errors and
        parsing goes on after each one, so one pass reports them all."""
        stmts = []
        while self.peek().kind != "EOF":
            stmt = self.declaration()
            if stmt is not None:
                stmts.append(stmt)
        return Program(stmts)

    def declaration(self):
        """One statement. After a syntax error it records the error, skips to
        a safe place, and returns None."""
        start = self.pos
        try:
            return self.statement()
        except ParseError as e:
            self.errors.append(e)
            self.synchronize(start)
            return None

    def synchronize(self, start):
        """Panic mode: skip to just after a ';', or to a token that starts a
        statement, or to a '}' (so the block around us can close). A block
        entered while skipping is skipped whole, up to its own '}'. Always
        moves at least one token, so parsing cannot get stuck."""
        depth = 0
        if self.pos == start:
            depth = self.skip(depth)
        while self.peek().kind != "EOF":
            if depth == 0:
                before = self.tokens[self.pos - 1]
                if before.kind == "OP" and before.text == ";":
                    return
                if self.at(*STATEMENT_START) or self.at("}"):
                    return
            depth = self.skip(depth)

    def skip(self, depth):
        """Consumes one token while recovering; returns the new block depth."""
        tok = self.advance()
        if tok.kind == "OP" and tok.text == "{":
            return depth + 1
        if tok.kind == "OP" and tok.text == "}" and depth > 0:
            return depth - 1
        return depth

    def statement(self):
        tok = self.peek()
        if tok.kind == "KEYWORD":
            if tok.text == "fn" and self.tokens[self.pos + 1].kind == "IDENT":
                return self.fn_decl()
            handler = {
                "let": self.let_stmt, "print": self.print_stmt, "if": self.if_stmt,
                "while": self.while_stmt, "for": self.for_stmt, "return": self.return_stmt,
                "break": self.jump_stmt, "continue": self.jump_stmt,
            }.get(tok.text)
            if handler is not None:
                return handler()
        return self.simple_stmt()

    def end_statement(self):
        self.expect(";")

    def name(self):
        tok = self.peek()
        if tok.kind != "IDENT":
            raise self.error(f"expected a name, found {describe(tok)}")
        return self.advance()

    def annotation(self, marker):
        """An optional type after ':' or '->'. Nothing checks types yet; they
        are notes for the reader."""
        if not self.at(marker):
            return None
        self.advance()
        tok = self.peek()
        if tok.kind != "IDENT" or tok.text not in TYPES:
            raise self.error(f"expected a type, found {describe(tok)}")
        return self.advance().text

    def let_stmt(self):
        self.advance()
        name = self.name()
        type_ = self.annotation(":")
        self.expect("=")
        value = self.expression()
        self.end_statement()
        return Let(name.text, type_, value, line=name.line, col=name.col)

    def print_stmt(self):
        tok = self.advance()
        value = self.expression()
        self.end_statement()
        return Print(value, line=tok.line, col=tok.col)

    def if_stmt(self):
        tok = self.advance()
        cond = self.expression()
        then = self.block()
        else_ = None
        if self.at("else"):
            self.advance()
            else_ = self.if_stmt() if self.at("if") else self.block()
        return If(cond, then, else_, line=tok.line, col=tok.col)

    def while_stmt(self):
        tok = self.advance()
        cond = self.expression()
        return While(cond, self.block(), line=tok.line, col=tok.col)

    def for_stmt(self):
        tok = self.advance()
        name = self.name()
        self.expect("in")
        iterable = self.expression()
        return For(name.text, iterable, self.block(), line=tok.line, col=tok.col)

    def return_stmt(self):
        tok = self.advance()
        value = None if self.at(";") else self.expression()
        self.end_statement()
        return Return(value, line=tok.line, col=tok.col)

    def jump_stmt(self):
        tok = self.advance()
        self.end_statement()
        kind = Break if tok.text == "break" else Continue
        return kind(line=tok.line, col=tok.col)

    def fn_decl(self):
        self.advance()
        name = self.name()
        params, ret, body = self.function_rest()
        return Fn(name.text, params, ret, body, line=name.line, col=name.col)

    def function_expr(self):
        tok = self.advance()
        params, ret, body = self.function_rest()
        return FnExpr(params, ret, body, line=tok.line, col=tok.col)

    def function_rest(self):
        """What follows 'fn' or 'fn name': parameters, return type, body."""
        self.expect("(")
        params = []
        if not self.at(")"):
            params.append(self.param())
            while self.at(","):
                self.advance()
                params.append(self.param())
        self.expect(")")
        ret = self.annotation("->")
        return params, ret, self.block()

    def param(self):
        name = self.name()
        return (name.text, self.annotation(":"))

    def block(self):
        tok = self.expect("{")
        stmts = []
        while not self.at("}"):
            if self.peek().kind == "EOF":
                raise self.error(f"expected '}}' to close the block opened at {tok.line}:{tok.col}, "
                                 f"found end of input")
            stmt = self.declaration()
            if stmt is not None:
                stmts.append(stmt)
        self.advance()
        return Block(stmts, line=tok.line, col=tok.col)

    def simple_stmt(self):
        """An assignment (to a name or an index) or an expression statement."""
        expr = self.expression()
        if self.at("="):
            eq = self.advance()
            value = self.expression()
            self.end_statement()
            if isinstance(expr, Var):
                return Assign(expr.name, value, line=expr.line, col=expr.col)
            if isinstance(expr, Index):
                return SetIndex(expr.target, expr.index, value, line=expr.line, col=expr.col)
            # The statement itself was well formed, so report without panicking.
            self.errors.append(self.error("can only assign to a name or an index", eq))
            return None
        self.end_statement()
        return ExprStmt(expr, line=expr.line, col=expr.col)


def parse_expression(source):
    """One expression and nothing after it. Raises the first LexError or ParseError."""
    parser = Parser(tokenize(source))
    expr = parser.expression()
    if parser.peek().kind != "EOF":
        raise parser.error(f"expected end of input, found {describe(parser.peek())}")
    return expr


def parse(source):
    """(program, errors). If the lexer found mistakes, errors are the lexer's
    and program is None: parsing broken tokens only adds confusing errors.
    Otherwise errors are the parser's, and the program must not run unless
    there are none."""
    tokens, errors = Lexer(source).scan()
    if errors:
        return None, errors
    parser = Parser(tokens)
    program = parser.program()
    return program, parser.errors


def quote(text):
    """A string as Comet source writes it: in quotes, with its escapes."""
    return '"' + text.replace("\\", "\\\\").replace('"', '\\"').replace("\n", "\\n") + '"'


def group(head, *parts):
    return "(" + " ".join([head, *parts]) + ")"


def sexpr(node):
    """The tree as a prefix expression, for tests and debugging:
    1 + 2 * x becomes (+ 1 (* 2 x))."""
    if isinstance(node, Num):
        return str(node.value)
    if isinstance(node, Str):
        return quote(node.value)
    if isinstance(node, Bool):
        return "true" if node.value else "false"
    if isinstance(node, Nil):
        return "nil"
    if isinstance(node, Var):
        return node.name
    if isinstance(node, Unary):
        return group(node.op, sexpr(node.expr))
    if isinstance(node, Binary):
        return group(node.op, sexpr(node.left), sexpr(node.right))
    if isinstance(node, Call):
        return group("call", sexpr(node.callee), *map(sexpr, node.args))
    if isinstance(node, Index):
        return group("index", sexpr(node.target), sexpr(node.index))
    if isinstance(node, ListLit):
        return group("list", *map(sexpr, node.items))
    if isinstance(node, MapLit):
        return group("map", *[sexpr(part) for pair in node.pairs for part in pair])
    return sexpr_statement(node)


def sexpr_statement(node):
    """sexpr for statements and functions: (let x 1), (block ...), ..."""
    if isinstance(node, (Fn, FnExpr)):
        params = "(" + " ".join(name for name, _type in node.params) + ")"
        head = ["fn", node.name] if isinstance(node, Fn) else ["fn"]
        return group(*head, params, sexpr(node.body))
    if isinstance(node, Let):
        return group("let", node.name, sexpr(node.expr))
    if isinstance(node, Assign):
        return group("set", node.name, sexpr(node.expr))
    if isinstance(node, SetIndex):
        return group("set", group("index", sexpr(node.target), sexpr(node.index)), sexpr(node.expr))
    if isinstance(node, Print):
        return group("print", sexpr(node.expr))
    if isinstance(node, ExprStmt):
        return group("expr", sexpr(node.expr))
    if isinstance(node, If):
        parts = [sexpr(node.cond), sexpr(node.then)]
        if node.else_ is not None:
            parts.append(sexpr(node.else_))
        return group("if", *parts)
    if isinstance(node, While):
        return group("while", sexpr(node.cond), sexpr(node.body))
    if isinstance(node, For):
        return group("for", node.name, sexpr(node.iterable), sexpr(node.body))
    if isinstance(node, Break):
        return "(break)"
    if isinstance(node, Continue):
        return "(continue)"
    if isinstance(node, Return):
        return "(return)" if node.expr is None else group("return", sexpr(node.expr))
    if isinstance(node, Block):
        return group("block", *map(sexpr, node.stmts))
    if isinstance(node, Program):
        return group("program", *map(sexpr, node.stmts))
    raise TypeError(f"sexpr cannot show {type(node).__name__}")


# ============================================================================
# The resolver: names and jumps, checked before anything runs
# ============================================================================

class ResolveError(StaticError):
    """A name or a jump used where it cannot be."""


class Resolver:
    """Checks names and jumps before the program runs, and records on each
    Var and Assign how many scopes out the declaration is (None: a global).

    It walks the tree exactly the way the interpreter will, opening a scope
    wherever the interpreter makes an Environment: for a block, for a call
    (the parameters and the body share one), and for each pass of a for loop
    (the loop variable and the body share one)."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.scopes = []      # innermost last; name -> ready (False while its initializer runs)
        self.errors = []
        self.functions = 0    # how many fns we are inside
        self.loops = 0        # how many loops we are inside, within the innermost fn

    def resolve(self, node):
        getattr(self, "visit_" + type(node).__name__)(node)

    def resolve_all(self, nodes):
        for node in nodes:
            self.resolve(node)

    def error(self, message, node):
        self.errors.append(ResolveError(message, node.line, node.col))

    def declare(self, name, node):
        if not self.scopes:
            return   # a global: declaring it again replaces it, which a REPL needs
        scope = self.scopes[-1]
        if name in scope:
            self.error(f"{name} is already declared in this scope", node)
        scope[name] = False

    def define(self, name):
        if self.scopes:
            self.scopes[-1][name] = True

    def resolve_local(self, node, name):
        """Records how many scopes out `name` lives; None if in none of them."""
        for i in range(len(self.scopes) - 1, -1, -1):
            if name in self.scopes[i]:
                node.depth = len(self.scopes) - 1 - i
                return
        node.depth = None   # looked up in the globals when it runs

    def function(self, node):
        outer_loops = self.loops
        self.functions += 1
        self.loops = 0        # a break inside a fn cannot leave a loop outside it
        scope = {}
        for name, _type in node.params:
            if name in scope:
                self.error(f"duplicate parameter {name}", node)
            scope[name] = True
        self.scopes.append(scope)
        self.resolve_all(node.body.stmts)
        self.scopes.pop()
        self.functions -= 1
        self.loops = outer_loops

    # ---- statements ----

    def visit_Program(self, node):
        self.resolve_all(node.stmts)

    def visit_Block(self, node):
        self.scopes.append({})
        self.resolve_all(node.stmts)
        self.scopes.pop()

    def visit_Let(self, node):
        self.declare(node.name, node)
        self.resolve(node.expr)
        self.define(node.name)

    def visit_Assign(self, node):
        self.resolve(node.expr)
        self.resolve_local(node, node.name)

    def visit_SetIndex(self, node):
        self.resolve_all([node.target, node.index, node.expr])

    def visit_Print(self, node):
        self.resolve(node.expr)

    visit_ExprStmt = visit_Print

    def visit_If(self, node):
        self.resolve(node.cond)
        self.resolve(node.then)
        if node.else_ is not None:
            self.resolve(node.else_)

    def visit_While(self, node):
        self.resolve(node.cond)
        self.loops += 1
        self.resolve(node.body)
        self.loops -= 1

    def visit_For(self, node):
        self.resolve(node.iterable)
        self.loops += 1
        self.scopes.append({node.name: True})
        self.resolve_all(node.body.stmts)
        self.scopes.pop()
        self.loops -= 1

    def visit_Break(self, node):
        if self.loops == 0:
            self.error("break outside a loop", node)

    def visit_Continue(self, node):
        if self.loops == 0:
            self.error("continue outside a loop", node)

    def visit_Return(self, node):
        if self.functions == 0:
            self.error("return outside a function", node)
        if node.expr is not None:
            self.resolve(node.expr)

    def visit_Fn(self, node):
        self.declare(node.name, node)
        self.define(node.name)    # before the body, so the fn can call itself
        self.function(node)

    # ---- expressions ----

    def visit_FnExpr(self, node):
        self.function(node)

    def visit_Var(self, node):
        if self.scopes and self.scopes[-1].get(node.name) is False:
            self.error(f"cannot read {node.name} in its own initializer", node)
        self.resolve_local(node, node.name)

    def visit_Num(self, node):
        pass

    visit_Str = visit_Bool = visit_Nil = visit_Num

    def visit_Unary(self, node):
        self.resolve(node.expr)

    def visit_Binary(self, node):
        self.resolve(node.left)
        self.resolve(node.right)

    def visit_Call(self, node):
        self.resolve(node.callee)
        self.resolve_all(node.args)

    def visit_Index(self, node):
        self.resolve(node.target)
        self.resolve(node.index)

    def visit_ListLit(self, node):
        self.resolve_all(node.items)

    def visit_MapLit(self, node):
        for key, value in node.pairs:
            self.resolve(key)
            self.resolve(value)


def resolve(program):
    """Resolves every name in program; returns the list of ResolveErrors."""
    resolver = Resolver()
    resolver.resolve(program)
    return resolver.errors


# ============================================================================
# Values
# ============================================================================

class CometError(Exception):
    """A runtime error in the Comet program (not a bug in the interpreter)."""


def comet_div(a, b):
    """Integer division that rounds toward zero, like C."""
    if b == 0:
        raise CometError("division by zero")
    q = abs(a) // abs(b)
    return q if (a < 0) == (b < 0) else -q


def comet_mod(a, b):
    return a - b * comet_div(a, b)


def type_name(value):
    """Comet's name for a value's type."""
    if value is None:
        return "nil"
    if isinstance(value, bool):     # before int: in Python, True is an int
        return "bool"
    if isinstance(value, int):
        return "int"
    if isinstance(value, str):
        return "str"
    if isinstance(value, Closure):
        return "fn"
    raise TypeError(f"not a Comet value: {value!r}")


def repr_value(value):
    """A value as Comet source writes it: strings in quotes."""
    if value is None:
        return "nil"
    if isinstance(value, bool):
        return "true" if value else "false"
    if isinstance(value, int):
        return str(value)
    if isinstance(value, str):
        return quote(value)
    if isinstance(value, Closure):
        return f"<fn {value.name}>" if value.name else "<fn>"
    raise TypeError(f"not a Comet value: {value!r}")


def show(value):
    """What print writes: a string as it is, anything else as repr_value."""
    return value if isinstance(value, str) else repr_value(value)


def values_equal(a, b):
    """Comet's ==: values of different types are never equal."""
    if type_name(a) != type_name(b):
        return False
    return a == b    # same Comet type, so Python's == is right (fns: the same fn)


ARITHMETIC = {
    "+": operator.add, "-": operator.sub, "*": operator.mul, "/": comet_div, "%": comet_mod,
    "<": operator.lt, "<=": operator.le, ">": operator.gt, ">=": operator.ge,
}
ORDERING = ("<", "<=", ">", ">=")
JOINABLE = ("str",)             # + also joins two of these


def arithmetic(op, left, right):
    """+ - * / % < <= > >= with Comet's type rules."""
    lt, rt = type_name(left), type_name(right)
    if lt == rt == "int":
        return ARITHMETIC[op](left, right)
    if op == "+" and lt == rt and lt in JOINABLE:
        return left + right
    if op in ORDERING and lt == rt == "str":
        return ARITHMETIC[op](left, right)
    raise CometError(f"'{op}' cannot combine {lt} and {rt}")


class Closure:
    """A Comet function value: its declaration (an Fn or FnExpr node) and
    the Environment it was made in, which it keeps alive."""

    def __init__(self, decl, env):
        self.decl = decl
        self.env = env

    @property
    def name(self):
        return self.decl.name if isinstance(self.decl, Fn) else None

    def label(self):
        return self.name or "anonymous fn"


class ReturnSignal(Exception):
    """Carries a return value up to the call waiting for it. Not a
    CometError, so nothing a Comet program does can catch it."""

    def __init__(self, value):
        self.value = value


def check_arity(name, fewest, most, got):
    if fewest <= got <= most:
        return
    if fewest == most:
        wanted = f"{fewest} argument" + ("" if fewest == 1 else "s")
    elif most == fewest + 1:
        wanted = f"{fewest} or {most} arguments"
    else:
        wanted = f"{fewest} to {most} arguments"
    raise CometError(f"{name} expects {wanted}, got {got}")


# ============================================================================
# The interpreter
# ============================================================================


class Environment:
    """One scope's variables, and the scope around it (None for the globals)."""

    def __init__(self, parent=None):
        self.values = {}
        self.parent = parent

    def define(self, name, value):
        if self.parent is not None and name in self.values:
            raise CometError(f"{name} is already declared in this scope")
        self.values[name] = value

    def lookup(self, name):
        env = self
        while env is not None:
            if name in env.values:
                return env.values[name]
            env = env.parent
        raise CometError(f"undefined variable {name}")

    def assign(self, name, value):
        env = self
        while env is not None:
            if name in env.values:
                env.values[name] = value
                return
            env = env.parent
        raise CometError(f"assignment to undeclared variable {name}")

    def ancestor(self, depth):
        """The scope `depth` steps out from this one."""
        env = self
        for _ in range(depth):
            env = env.parent
        return env


class Interpreter:
    """Runs a syntax tree. Printed lines collect in self.output."""

    def __init__(self):
        self.globals = Environment()
        self.env = self.globals       # the scope running now
        self.output = []

    def run(self, program):
        for stmt in program.stmts:
            self.execute(stmt)

    def handler(self, prefix, node):
        """The method for this kind of node: exec_Print for a Print, and so on."""
        method = getattr(self, prefix + type(node).__name__, None)
        if method is None:
            raise CometError(f"{type(node).__name__} is not supported yet")
        return method

    def execute(self, stmt):
        self.handler("exec_", stmt)(stmt)

    def evaluate(self, expr):
        return self.handler("eval_", expr)(expr)

    def execute_block(self, stmts, env):
        """Runs stmts with env as the current scope, and always puts the old
        scope back, also when a statement raises."""
        previous = self.env
        self.env = env
        try:
            for stmt in stmts:
                self.execute(stmt)
        finally:
            self.env = previous

    # ---- statements ----

    def exec_Let(self, stmt):
        self.env.define(stmt.name, self.evaluate(stmt.expr))

    def exec_Assign(self, stmt):
        value = self.evaluate(stmt.expr)
        if stmt.depth is None:
            self.globals.assign(stmt.name, value)
        else:
            self.env.ancestor(stmt.depth).values[stmt.name] = value

    def exec_Print(self, stmt):
        self.output.append(show(self.evaluate(stmt.expr)))

    def exec_ExprStmt(self, stmt):
        self.evaluate(stmt.expr)

    def exec_If(self, stmt):
        if self.condition(stmt.cond):
            self.execute(stmt.then)
        elif stmt.else_ is not None:
            self.execute(stmt.else_)    # a Block, or an If for "else if"

    def exec_While(self, stmt):
        while self.condition(stmt.cond):
            self.execute(stmt.body)

    def exec_Block(self, stmt):
        self.execute_block(stmt.stmts, Environment(self.env))

    def condition(self, expr):
        value = self.evaluate(expr)
        if not isinstance(value, bool):
            raise CometError(f"a condition must be bool, not {type_name(value)}")
        return value

    # ---- expressions ----

    def eval_Num(self, expr):
        return expr.value

    eval_Str = eval_Bool = eval_Num

    def eval_Nil(self, expr):
        return None

    def eval_Var(self, expr):
        if expr.depth is None:
            return self.globals.lookup(expr.name)
        return self.env.ancestor(expr.depth).values[expr.name]

    def eval_Unary(self, expr):
        value = self.evaluate(expr.expr)
        if expr.op == "-":
            self.need("int", value, "-")
            return -value
        self.need("bool", value, "not")
        return not value

    def need(self, wanted, value, op):
        if type_name(value) != wanted:
            raise CometError(f"'{op}' needs {wanted}, not {type_name(value)}")

    def eval_Binary(self, expr):
        op = expr.op
        left = self.evaluate(expr.left)
        if op in ("and", "or"):
            self.need("bool", left, op)
            if left == (op == "or"):     # false and ..., true or ...: already decided
                return left
            right = self.evaluate(expr.right)
            self.need("bool", right, op)
            return right
        right = self.evaluate(expr.right)
        if op in ("==", "!="):
            lt, rt = type_name(left), type_name(right)
            if lt != rt and "nil" not in (lt, rt):
                raise CometError(f"cannot compare {lt} with {rt}")
            return values_equal(left, right) == (op == "==")
        return arithmetic(op, left, right)

    # ---- functions ----

    def exec_Fn(self, stmt):
        self.env.define(stmt.name, Closure(stmt, self.env))

    def eval_FnExpr(self, expr):
        return Closure(expr, self.env)

    def exec_Return(self, stmt):
        value = None if stmt.expr is None else self.evaluate(stmt.expr)
        raise ReturnSignal(value)

    def eval_Call(self, expr):
        callee = self.evaluate(expr.callee)
        args = [self.evaluate(arg) for arg in expr.args]
        return self.call(callee, args)

    def call(self, callee, args):
        """Calls a function value with argument values, and returns its result."""
        if isinstance(callee, Closure):
            params = callee.decl.params
            check_arity(callee.label(), len(params), len(params), len(args))
            env = Environment(callee.env)   # inside the fn's own scope, not the caller's
            for (name, _type), value in zip(params, args):
                env.define(name, value)
            try:
                self.execute_block(callee.decl.body.stmts, env)
            except ReturnSignal as signal:
                return signal.value
            return None
        raise CometError(f"cannot call a value of type {type_name(callee)}")


def run(source):
    """Runs a Comet program and returns what it printed, one line per print.
    Errors found before running are the whole answer; a runtime error is
    added after whatever was printed before it."""
    program, errors = parse(source)
    if not errors:
        errors = resolve(program)
    if errors:
        return "\n".join(str(e) for e in errors)
    interp = Interpreter()
    try:
        interp.run(program)
    except CometError as e:
        interp.output.append(f"runtime error: {e}")
    return "\n".join(interp.output)
--- hint
Give the resolver `scopes` (a list of dicts), `errors`, and counters `functions` and `loops`, and one `visit_<Node>` method per node class, found with `getattr` like the interpreter's handlers. Expressions just resolve their children; literals do nothing.
--- hint
For a use, search `range(len(self.scopes) - 1, -1, -1)` and set `node.depth = len(self.scopes) - 1 - i` at the first scope that has the name; `None` if none does. A function: save `loops`, add one to `functions`, set `loops = 0`, push a scope with the parameters, resolve `body.stmts`, pop, and restore both counters.
--- hint
`declare` does nothing at the top level (no scopes) and reports a name that the innermost scope already has. `visit_Var` reports the own-initializer error when the innermost scope maps the name to `False`. In the interpreter, `ancestor` is a loop of `env = env.parent`, `depth` times.

+++ practice | Depths for a block language
--- task
A toy program is a list whose items are either strings `"let NAME"` and `"use NAME"`, or a nested list, which is a block (a new scope). The outermost list is the global level, which is **not** a scope.

Write `resolve_depths(program)` that returns, for every `use` in order, a pair `(NAME, depth)`: the number of block scopes outwards from the innermost one to the one declaring the name, or `None` if no enclosing block declares it (a global, or undeclared). A name counts as declared from its `let` onwards.

For example, `resolve_depths(["let a", ["let b", "use b", ["use b", "use a"]]])` is `[("b", 0), ("b", 1), ("a", None)]`.
--- starter
def resolve_depths(program):
    return []
--- solution
def resolve_depths(program):
    out = []
    scopes = []

    def walk(items):
        for item in items:
            if isinstance(item, list):
                scopes.append(set())
                walk(item)
                scopes.pop()
                continue
            kind, name = item.split()
            if kind == "let":
                if scopes:
                    scopes[-1].add(name)
            else:
                depth = None
                for i in range(len(scopes) - 1, -1, -1):
                    if name in scopes[i]:
                        depth = len(scopes) - 1 - i
                        break
                out.append((name, depth))

    walk(program)
    return out
--- hint
Keep a stack of sets, one per open block, innermost last. The global level adds nothing to it.
--- hint
Search the stack from the end: the first set with the name gives the depth `len(scopes) - 1 - i`.
--- check case | The example
resolve_depths(["let a", ["let b", "use b", ["use b", "use a"]]])
=> [("b", 0), ("b", 1), ("a", None)]
--- check case | A use before the let in the same block is not the local one
resolve_depths([["let x", ["use x", "let x", "use x"]]])
=> [("x", 1), ("x", 0)]
--- check case | Sibling blocks do not see each other
resolve_depths([["let s"], ["use s"], "use s"])
=> [("s", None), ("s", None)]
--- check case | Deep nesting
resolve_depths([["let t", [[["use t"]]]]])
=> [("t", 3)]
--- check case | Nothing to resolve
resolve_depths([])
=> []

+++ practice | Unused local variables
--- task
Using the same toy format as a block language (`"let NAME"`, `"use NAME"`, nested lists as blocks, the outer list global and not a scope), write `unused_locals(program)` that returns the names of local variables that are declared but never used, in the order they were declared. A use counts for the nearest enclosing declaration of that name that comes before it (in the same block or an outer block). Globals are never reported.

For example, `unused_locals([["let a", "let b", "use a"], "let g"])` is `["b"]`.
--- starter
def unused_locals(program):
    return []
--- solution
def unused_locals(program):
    declared = []
    scopes = []

    def walk(items):
        for item in items:
            if isinstance(item, list):
                scopes.append({})
                walk(item)
                scopes.pop()
                continue
            kind, name = item.split()
            if kind == "let":
                if scopes:
                    record = [name, False]
                    declared.append(record)
                    scopes[-1][name] = record
            else:
                for scope in reversed(scopes):
                    if name in scope:
                        scope[name][1] = True
                        break

    walk(program)
    return [name for name, used in declared if not used]
--- hint
Give each declaration a small record (its name and a "used" flag) and keep the records in a list in declaration order. Each scope maps names to their records.
--- hint
A new `let` of the same name in the same block replaces the scope's entry, so later uses mark the newer declaration.
--- check case | The example
unused_locals([["let a", "let b", "use a"], "let g"])
=> ["b"]
--- check case | A use in an inner block counts, a use after the block does not
unused_locals([["let a", ["use a"], "let c"], "use c"])
=> ["c"]
--- check case | Shadowing: the inner declaration is the one used
unused_locals([["let x", ["let x", "use x"]]])
=> ["x"]
--- check case | Redeclared in the same block, only the second is used
unused_locals([["let n", "let n", "use n"]])
=> ["n"]
--- check case | Nothing local
unused_locals(["let a", "use a", "use zz"])
=> []

+++ practice | Checking where jumps are allowed
--- task
A program is a list of statements, each a tuple: `("break",)`, `("continue",)`, `("return",)`, `("loop", [body])` and `("fn", [body])`. Write `jump_errors(program)` that returns a list of messages, in program order:

- `"break outside a loop"` and `"continue outside a loop"` when there is no enclosing loop **inside the innermost enclosing function** (a function's body cannot break out of a loop around the function);
- `"return outside a function"` when there is no enclosing function.

For example, `jump_errors([("loop", [("fn", [("break",)])]), ("return",)])` is `["break outside a loop", "return outside a function"]`.
--- starter
def jump_errors(program):
    return []
--- solution
def jump_errors(program):
    errors = []

    def walk(stmts, loops, functions):
        for stmt in stmts:
            kind = stmt[0]
            if kind == "loop":
                walk(stmt[1], loops + 1, functions)
            elif kind == "fn":
                walk(stmt[1], 0, functions + 1)
            elif kind in ("break", "continue"):
                if loops == 0:
                    errors.append(f"{kind} outside a loop")
            elif functions == 0:
                errors.append("return outside a function")

    walk(program, 0, 0)
    return errors
--- hint
Walk the statements carrying two counts: loops inside the current function, and functions.
--- hint
Entering a function passes a loop count of 0 to its body; entering a loop adds one.
--- check case | The example
jump_errors([("loop", [("fn", [("break",)])]), ("return",)])
=> ["break outside a loop", "return outside a function"]
--- check case | Everything in its place
jump_errors([("fn", [("loop", [("break",), ("continue",), ("loop", [("break",)])]), ("return",)])])
=> []
--- check case | A loop inside a function inside a loop
jump_errors([("loop", [("fn", [("continue",), ("loop", [("continue",)]), ("return",)]), ("break",)])])
=> ["continue outside a loop"]
--- check case | Empty program, and top-level jumps
(jump_errors([]), jump_errors([("continue",), ("break",)]))
=> ([], ["continue outside a loop", "break outside a loop"])

+++ practice | Declarations checked in scope
--- task
Statements are tuples: `("let", NAME, [names read by the initializer])`, `("use", NAME)` and `("block", [statements])`. The top level is global; each block is a local scope. Write `scope_errors(program)` that returns, in order:

- `"NAME declared twice"` for a `let` of a name that the **same local** block already declared (redeclaring a global is allowed);
- `"NAME read in its own initializer"` when a local `let`'s initializer reads the name it declares (at the top level this is allowed: it means the old global).

Declarations that are fine in an inner block, such as shadowing an outer name, are not errors. For example, `scope_errors([("block", [("let", "a", []), ("let", "a", ["a"])])])` is `["a declared twice", "a read in its own initializer"]`.
--- starter
def scope_errors(program):
    return []
--- solution
def scope_errors(program):
    errors = []

    def walk(stmts, local):
        declared = set()
        for stmt in stmts:
            kind = stmt[0]
            if kind == "block":
                walk(stmt[1], True)
            elif kind == "let":
                name = stmt[1]
                if local and name in declared:
                    errors.append(f"{name} declared twice")
                if local and name in stmt[2]:
                    errors.append(f"{name} read in its own initializer")
                declared.add(name)

    walk(program, False)
    return errors
--- hint
Each block has its own set of names declared so far. Pass a flag saying whether you are at the top level.
--- hint
Check "declared twice" before adding the name, and check the initializer's names against the name being declared.
--- check case | The example
scope_errors([("block", [("let", "a", []), ("let", "a", ["a"])])])
=> ["a declared twice", "a read in its own initializer"]
--- check case | Globals may be redeclared and may read themselves
scope_errors([("let", "g", []), ("let", "g", ["g"])])
=> []
--- check case | Shadowing in an inner block is fine
scope_errors([("block", [("let", "x", []), ("block", [("let", "x", ["x"])])])])
=> ["x read in its own initializer"]
--- check case | Sibling blocks have separate scopes

=> []

+++ practice | Debug: depths counted from the wrong end
--- task
`depths(program)` computes resolver depths for the toy block format (`"let NAME"`, `"use NAME"`, nested lists as blocks, the outer list global and not a scope), returning a `(NAME, depth)` pair for each use, with `None` for names in no block. It passes a test with one level of nesting but gives wrong depths deeper down: `depths([["let a", ["use a"]]])` should be `[("a", 1)]` but it gives `[("a", 0)]`. Fix it.
--- starter
def depths(program):

--- solution
def depths(program):
    out = []
    scopes = []

    def walk(items):
        for item in items:
            if isinstance(item, list):
                scopes.append(set())
                walk(item)
                scopes.pop()
            elif item.startswith("let "):
                if scopes:
                    scopes[-1].add(item[4:])
            else:
                name = item[4:]
                found = None
                for i in range(len(scopes) - 1, -1, -1):
                    if name in scopes[i]:
                        found = len(scopes) - 1 - i
                        break
                out.append((name, found))

    walk(program)
    return out
--- hint
`i` is the scope's position counted from the **outermost** block. What does a depth count from?
--- hint
A depth is how many scopes out from the innermost one: for a stack of k scopes, position i is k − 1 − i steps out.
--- check case | The example

=> [("a", 2), ("b", 1), ("c", None)]

+++ practice | Slots: a variable as two numbers
--- task
Compilers turn each local variable into a pair `(depth, slot)`: the depth as before, and the slot, the variable's position among the declarations of its scope (the first `let` in a block is slot 0, the next slot 1, and so on). The interpreter can then keep each scope's values in a list instead of a dictionary.

Using the toy format (`"let NAME"`, `"use NAME"`, nested lists as blocks, the outer list global and not a scope), write `slots(program)` that returns, for every `use` in order, `(NAME, depth, slot)`, or `(NAME, None, None)` for a name in no enclosing block. A block that declares the same name twice gives the second declaration a new slot, and later uses refer to it.

For example, `slots([["let a", "let b", ["let c", "use a", "use c"]]])` is `[("a", 1, 0), ("c", 0, 0)]`.
--- starter
def slots(program):
    return []
--- solution
def slots(program):
    out = []
    scopes = []

    def walk(items):
        for item in items:
            if isinstance(item, list):
                scopes.append({})
                walk(item)
                scopes.pop()
                continue
            kind, name = item.split()
            if kind == "let":
                if scopes:
                    scope = scopes[-1]
                    scope[name] = max(scope.values(), default=-1) + 1   # slots only grow
                continue
            for i in range(len(scopes) - 1, -1, -1):
                if name in scopes[i]:
                    out.append((name, len(scopes) - 1 - i, scopes[i][name]))
                    break
            else:
                out.append((name, None, None))

    walk(program)
    return out
--- hint
Each scope maps a name to its slot. Slots are handed out in order and only grow, so the next slot is one more than the largest given so far (0 for the first).
--- hint
The depth comes from where you find the name in the stack, as before; the slot comes from that scope's map.
--- check case | The example
slots([["let a", "let b", ["let c", "use a", "use c"]]])
=> [("a", 1, 0), ("c", 0, 0)]
--- check case | A redeclared name gets a new slot
slots([["let x", "let y", "let x", "let z", "use x", "use y", "use z"]])
=> [("x", 0, 2), ("y", 0, 1), ("z", 0, 3)]
--- check case | Globals and undeclared names
slots(["let g", "use g", ["use g"]])
=> [("g", None, None), ("g", None, None)]
--- check case | Separate blocks restart their slots
slots([["let a", "let b", "use b"], ["let c", "use c"]])
=> [("b", 0, 1), ("c", 0, 0)]

=== cap-interp-07 | Lists, for loops, break and continue
--- teach
The language core is complete and sound: values, scopes resolved before running, functions and closures. Everything from here on is new Comet. This milestone adds its first data structure, the **list**, the `for` loop that walks through one, `break` and `continue`, and the first two **builtins**, functions written in Python that Comet programs can call: `len` and `push`. The parser has understood all of this syntax since milestone 3; now it gets a meaning.

### What a list is

A **list** is an ordered, changeable sequence of values of any types: `[1, "two", [3], nil]`. The interpreter represents a Comet list as a Python list. Its type name is `list`, and it prints with each item written by `repr_value`, so strings inside keep their quotes:

```text
print [1, "a b", [true], nil];      # [1, "a b", [true], nil]
```

That is why `repr_value` exists apart from `show`: `print "a b";` writes `a b`, but inside a list the quotes are what tell you where one string ends.

- `eval_ListLit` evaluates the items from left to right and returns a new list.
- `xs[i]` reads an item, and `xs[i] = v;` replaces one. The index must be an **int** (and `true` is not an int), and it must satisfy 0 ≤ i < length. Comet has no negative indexes: `xs[-1]` is an error, not the last item. That is a deliberate choice. In Python an index computed as `i - 1` that reaches -1 by mistake silently reads the last item; in Comet it stops with a message.
- `a + b` on two lists makes a **new** list, like strings.

The messages are exact, because tests and people depend on them: `an index must be int, not bool`, `index 3 out of range for a list of length 3`, `cannot index a value of type int`.

### Lists are shared, not copied

A variable does not hold a list; it holds a **reference** to one. Assigning, passing to a function, or putting a list inside another list copies the reference, not the items:

```text
let a = [1, 2];
let b = a;
b[0] = 99;
print a;          # [99, 2]
```

This is called **aliasing**: two names for one object. It is how Python, JavaScript and Java treat their lists too, and it is why `push` can work at all: `push(xs, 4)` changes the list that `xs` refers to, and everyone holding that reference sees the change. Using Python's own lists gives Comet exactly these semantics for free.

Equality is different. `==` on two lists compares them **item by item**: two separate lists with equal items are equal. `values_equal` becomes recursive: same type, same length, and every pair of items equal by the same rules. So `[1] == [true]` is `false`, because 1 and `true` have different types, even though Python says `[1] == [True]`.

### The for loop

`for x in xs { … }` runs its body once per item. Two design decisions matter here.

**A fresh variable for every pass.** Each pass makes a new environment holding `x`, and the body's statements run directly in it, which is the scope the resolver already opens for a `for`. So a closure made in the body captures that pass's `x`, not a single variable shared by all passes:

```text
let getters = [];
for n in [10, 20] {
  push(getters, fn () { return n; });
}
print getters[0]();      # 10
```

With one shared variable, both closures would return 20. JavaScript's `var` behaved that way and caused bugs for twenty years, until `let` in [[for loops got a fresh binding|jsloop]] per pass.

**Walk a snapshot.** Before the first pass, `iteration(value)` copies the list, and the loop walks the copy. So a body that pushes to the list it is walking cannot loop forever, and one that removes items cannot make the loop skip any. The cost is O(n) extra memory per loop. The alternative, walking the live list, is what Python does, and changing a list while iterating over it is one of the classic Python bugs.

`iteration` is also where a later milestone lets `for` walk strings and maps. Anything else is `cannot loop over a value of type int`.

### break and continue

`break` leaves the innermost loop; `continue` skips to its next pass. They are implemented exactly like `return`: `exec_Break` raises `BreakSignal`, `exec_Continue` raises `ContinueSignal`, and each loop catches them around its body. `while` and `for` both need it.

- The signals pass up through any blocks in between, and each block's `finally` restores its environment on the way.
- They are not `CometError`s, for the same reason as `ReturnSignal`.
- A `break` can never escape its function: the resolver already rejects a `break` that is not inside a loop in the same function. So the interpreter never needs to handle a stray signal.

### Builtins

Some operations cannot be written in Comet at all, such as the length of a list, and others are much faster in Python. A **builtin** is a function written in Python and made available to Comet programs as an ordinary global value. The starter gives the machinery:

- `Builtin(name, fn, arity)`, a value like a closure: its type name is `fn`, and it prints as `<builtin len>`. `arity` is a number, or a pair `(fewest, most)`; the class stores `fewest` and `most`.
- `BUILTINS`, a dictionary from name to `(fn, arity)`, filled by a **decorator**: writing `@builtin("len", 1)` above a Python function registers it. See the [[decorator note|decorator]].
- `expect_type(name, value, *kinds)`, which raises `len needs list or str, not int` when the value's type is not one of the kinds.

Every builtin's Python function gets the interpreter first and then the Comet arguments, so `builtin_push(interp, items, value)`. Most builtins ignore the interpreter; a later milestone needs it for builtins that call Comet functions back.

Two changes connect them to the interpreter:

1. `Interpreter.__init__` defines every entry of `BUILTINS` in the globals, as a `Builtin` value. So builtins are globals, found by the resolver's "not local, so global" rule, and a program may shadow them: `let len = 3;` is allowed.
2. `call` accepts a `Builtin`: check the arity with `check_arity(name, fewest, most, got)`, then return `fn(self, *args)`.

This milestone's two builtins: `len(x)` for a list or string, and `push(list, value)`, which appends in place and returns `nil`.

### Why it is correct

- **Indexing:** `checked_index` accepts exactly the ints i with 0 ≤ i < length, so an item is read or written only at a position that exists; everything else is a Comet error with a message, never a Python `IndexError`.
- **for:** the loop walks a copy made before the first pass, so it runs exactly once per item the list had when the loop started, whatever the body does to the list. Each pass binds a new variable, so a closure made in pass k sees item k.
- **Signals:** a `BreakSignal` raised in a body is caught by the nearest loop around it in the same function, because the resolver rejects any other placement, and loops catch it before anything else can.

### What it costs

Indexing, replacing and `push` are O(1) (push is amortised O(1): Python lists grow by [[over-allocating|overalloc]], like the dynamic array of DSA I). `+` on lists builds a new list, O(n + m), so building a list by `xs = xs + [x]` in a loop is O(n²); `push` is O(n) for the same job. A `for` loop costs O(n) for the snapshot plus its body. `==` on lists is O(total size).

### How to test it

Print literals, nested lists and strings inside lists; read and write items; show aliasing through a second name and through a function parameter; each index error; `+` leaving both operands unchanged; equality with nested lists and bools; `for` with closures, with a body that pushes to its own list, and with `break` and `continue` in nested loops; each builtin, its type errors and its arity error.

### Where it is used

- Every scripting language has a growable list with these semantics: Python's `list`, JavaScript's `Array`, Ruby's `Array`, Lua's tables.
- A telemetry pipeline keeps the latest readings in exactly such a list, pushing each new sample and looping over a snapshot to compute averages, while new samples keep arriving.

**Watch out:** list bugs in an interpreter.

- Accepting a bool as an index: in Python `xs[True]` is `xs[1]`.
- Letting a negative index through, so `xs[-1]` quietly works.
- Comparing lists with Python's `==`, so `[1] == [true]` is true.
- Looping over the live list: a body that pushes to it never ends.
- Making the loop variable once, outside the loop, so every closure made in the body sees the last item.

::: context jsloop Closures in loops, in JavaScript
Before 2015, JavaScript's only variable declaration was `var`, whose scope is the whole function. A loop that created click handlers, one per button, gave every handler the same variable, so every button reported the last index. The standard fix was an extra function call per pass, just to create a new scope. ES2015 added `let`, and specified that a `for` loop with `let` creates a fresh binding for every pass: exactly Comet's rule.
:::

::: context decorator How @builtin works
A decorator is a function applied to the function defined just below it. `@builtin("len", 1)` first calls `builtin("len", 1)`, which returns a small function `register`; Python then calls `register(builtin_len)` and stores whatever it returns under the name `builtin_len`. Here `register` records the function in `BUILTINS` and returns it unchanged. So adding a builtin is one decorated function, anywhere in the file, with no list to edit elsewhere.
:::

::: context overalloc Why push is fast
A Python list keeps its items in one block of memory with spare room at the end. Appending uses the spare room; when it runs out, CPython allocates a bigger block, about an eighth bigger plus a little, and copies the items across. Because the block grows by a fixed fraction, the copies add up to O(n) over n appends, so each append costs O(1) on average: the amortised argument from DSA I.
:::
--- task
The starter gives `Builtin(name, fn, arity)` (with `fewest`, `most` and `label()`), `BreakSignal`, `ContinueSignal`, the tuples `SEQUENCES = ("list",)` and `SIZED = ("list", "str")`, the `BUILTINS` registry with the `@builtin(name, arity)` decorator, and `expect_type(name, value, *kinds)`. Write:

- Lists as Python lists: `type_name` gives `"list"`, and a `Builtin` is also `"fn"`; `repr_value` writes `[` items with `repr_value` separated by `, ` `]`, and a builtin as `<builtin NAME>`; `values_equal` compares lists item by item (same length, every pair equal by `values_equal`); `+` also joins two lists into a new list (`JOINABLE = ("str", "list")`).
- `checked_index(seq, index)`: return the index if it is an int with `0 <= index < len(seq)`; otherwise raise `an index must be int, not T` or `index I out of range for a TYPE of length N` (TYPE is `type_name(seq)`).
- `get_item(target, index)`: for a type in `SEQUENCES`, the item at the checked index; otherwise `cannot index a value of type T`.
- `set_item(target, index, value)`: for a list, replace the item at the checked index; otherwise `cannot index a value of type T`.
- `iteration(value)`: for a list, a copy of it; otherwise `cannot loop over a value of type T`.
- `eval_ListLit`; `eval_Index` (evaluate the target, then the index); `exec_SetIndex` (evaluate the target, the index, then the value); `exec_For` (for each item of `iteration(...)`, a new `Environment(self.env)` with the loop variable defined in it, the body's statements run in it with `execute_block`); `exec_Break` and `exec_Continue` raising the signals; and `break`/`continue` handling in both `while` and `for`.
- In `Interpreter.__init__`, define every `BUILTINS` entry in the globals as `Builtin(name, fn, arity)`. In `call`, a `Builtin` checks its arity with `check_arity(callee.name, callee.fewest, callee.most, len(args))` and returns `callee.fn(self, *args)`.
- `builtin_len(interp, value)` registered as `len` with arity 1: the length of a type in `SIZED`, else `expect_type`'s error. `builtin_push(interp, items, value)` registered as `push` with arity 2: append to a list and return `None`; not a list gives `push needs list, not T`.
--- starter
"""Comet: a small programming language, built in layers.

    source text -> Lexer -> tokens -> Parser -> syntax tree
                -> Resolver -> Interpreter -> printed output

Each layer only talks to the one after it, so each can be tested alone.
"""
import operator
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


# ============================================================================
# Tokens and the lexer
# ============================================================================

KEYWORDS = {
    "let", "fn", "return", "if", "else", "while", "for", "in", "break",
    "continue", "print", "true", "false", "nil", "and", "or", "not",
}
TWO_CHAR = {"==", "!=", "<=", ">=", "->"}
ONE_CHAR = set("+-*/%<>=(){}[],;:")
ESCAPES = {'"': '"', "\\": "\\", "n": "\n"}
DIGITS = set("0123456789")
LETTERS = set("abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ_")
# Characters people type from other languages, and what Comet wants instead.
LEX_HINTS = {
    "'": "strings use double quotes",
    "&": "use 'and'",
    "|": "use 'or'",
    "!": "use 'not', or '!=' for not equal",
}


@dataclass
class Token:
    kind: str   # NUMBER, STRING, IDENT, KEYWORD, OP or EOF
    text: str   # the source text; for a STRING, the decoded value
    line: int   # counted from 1
    col: int    # counted from 1


class StaticError(Exception):
    """A mistake found before the program runs. Prints as "line:col: message"."""

    def __init__(self, message, line, col):
        super().__init__(f"{line}:{col}: {message}")
        self.message = message
        self.line = line
        self.col = col


class LexError(StaticError):
    """A character sequence that is not a Comet token."""


class Lexer:
    """Turns source text into tokens. It keeps going after a mistake, so one
    scan reports every lexing error, each with its line and column."""

    def __init__(self, source):
        self.source = source
        self.pos = 0          # index of the next character to read
        self.line = 1         # where that character is, for messages
        self.col = 1
        self.tokens = []
        self.errors = []

    def peek(self, ahead=0):
        """A character ahead of the read position, or "" past the end."""
        i = self.pos + ahead
        return self.source[i] if i < len(self.source) else ""

    def advance(self):
        """Consumes one character and keeps line and col in step with it."""
        ch = self.source[self.pos]
        self.pos += 1
        if ch == "\n":
            self.line += 1
            self.col = 1
        else:
            self.col += 1
        return ch

    def scan(self):
